## Chapter 1: Project Overview and Motivation

### 1.1 Problem statement — what does indoor LIDAR mapping solve?

Indoor floor plans of small to medium spaces — single rooms, apartments,
small offices, workshops — are routinely needed for purposes ranging from
furniture planning and renovation to robotic navigation seeding, building
management, and exploration of unknown environments. Traditional
approaches to producing such a plan involve either tape-measure-and-pencil
surveying, photogrammetric reconstruction from many images, or expensive
commercial scanners. The first is tedious and error-prone, the second
requires a controlled lighting environment and substantial post-processing,
and the third is cost-prohibitive for one-off domestic or hobbyist use.

The Recon-Platform-R2 project addresses this gap with a **handheld
two-dimensional LIDAR scanner** that the operator carries through the
space at walking pace. As the device moves, a 360° spinning LIDAR
acquires range data, an on-device Simultaneous Localisation And Mapping
(SLAM) algorithm consumes those scans and continuously rebuilds a
top-down occupancy grid, and an embedded web user interface lets the
operator observe the map filling in live, save snapshots to a local
database, and post-process saved maps into cleaned vector floor plans.
No external infrastructure is required at runtime: the device runs its
own WiFi access point so any smartphone or laptop can connect directly
to it in the field.

The mapping algorithm produces a **two-dimensional occupancy grid** rather
than a three-dimensional point cloud or mesh. This is a deliberate
limitation: 2-D representations are sufficient for floor-plan-style
visualisations, slam_toolbox is mature in the 2-D regime, and the cost,
weight, computational requirement, and complexity of a 3-D solution
(tilting LIDAR, structured-light depth camera, or photogrammetric
fusion) are substantially higher. Where height varies inside the scanned
volume — staircases, mezzanines, lofted ceilings — the device records
only the slice of the world that lies in its horizontal scanning plane.

### 1.3 Project evolution: from autonomous robot to handheld scanner

The repository carries forward git history from an earlier incarnation of
the project — an autonomous mobile robot codenamed *roomba*. The pivot
was decided on 2026-05-09 and executed across commits `5088514` (H1) and
`6c315cb` (H1.5) on 2026-05-10. The pre-pivot documentation is preserved
verbatim in `docs/archive/2026-05-10_pre-handheld/` with deprecation
headers on each file. The archive holds four canonical files:
`rules.md`, `project_requirements.md`, `project_status.md` and
`esp32_firmware.md`.

The transition discarded a substantial fraction of the codebase. The
following subsystems existed in the pre-pivot version and have been
removed:

* **Motor control.** The H-bridge driver (DRV8833 or L298N variant) and
  the ESP32-as-motor-coprocessor I²C protocol at address `0x42` are gone.
  The ESP32 has been re-purposed as a USB-Serial sensor and actuator hub
  with no motor responsibilities.
* **Bluetooth + Xbox controller stack.** `xpadneo`, `bluez`,
  `joy_linux_node`, `joy_control_node`, `bluetooth_manager.py`, the
  Controller and Bluetooth pages of the web UI, the `bt_sim_node` and
  all related mock devices have been deleted.
* **Autonomous navigation.** The entire `roomba_navigation` package
  containing `recon_node` (a Mamdani fuzzy frontier explorer with 15
  rules) and `sim_goal_follower` (a P-controller with fuzzy
  obstacle-avoidance) is gone. `nav2` was never integrated.
* **Simulated kinematics.** The `sim_motor_node` and its diff-drive
  kinematics + collision-detection code paths were removed; the
  pre-pivot `sim_sensor_node` shrank from 952 lines to its current 463.
* **Web UI controller and Bluetooth pages.** The four-page UI
  (Dashboard, Controller, Bluetooth, Map) was reduced to two, then
  reshuffled into the current set (Map at `/`, Saved at `/maps`,
  Diagnostics at `/diagnostics`, with `/map` and `/stats` kept as 301
  redirects for back-compatibility).
* **Pose topic name.** `/roomba/pose` was renamed to `/scanner/pose`.
* **Environment variable name.** `ROOMBA_DB_URL` was renamed to
  `RECON_DB_URL`. The PostgreSQL container name and its database/user
  credentials remained `roomba_postgres` / `roomba` / `roomba` so that
  historical scan data already in the Docker volume on the developer's
  Pi was not orphaned (`AGENT_RULES.md` §5 documents this carry-over).

Several architectural patterns survived the pivot essentially unchanged
and account for much of the residual sophistication of the codebase:

* The **mock-fallback architecture** in `recon_webui.data_channels` —
  every data source is wrapped in a `DataChannel` that returns the most
  recent real ROS2 message when one has been received within a
  configurable timeout, and a mock value otherwise. There is no
  LIVE/DEMO mode flag and no client-side branching. The pre-pivot
  design notes (`project_requirements.md` rev 1.6) describe this as a
  deliberate architectural choice; the implementation in the current
  `data_channels.py` is byte-for-byte the same pattern, modulo
  defensive handling of the eventlet-greened `threading` module
  (described in §8.1 below).
* The **eventlet threading invariants** (`monkey_patch()` first;
  `socketio.emit()` only from the eventlet hub; `tpool.execute()` for
  blocking calls in Flask routes) survived the pivot and are now
  enshrined in `docs/AGENT_RULES.md` §6 as binding rules.
* The **headless save pipeline** that allows a hardware button press to
  cause a map save via the `db_node` subscription to `/robot/events`
  predates the pivot. The path is still in `db_node.py` and is
  triggered from the ESP32 SAVE button (after firmware Inc 2 routes the
  hardware event through `esp32_uart_bridge`).

### 1.4 Scope limitations and deliberate design exclusions

The system is deliberately narrow. The following classes of feature are
**explicitly excluded** and will not be added without a corresponding
revision of the project specification:

* **Three-dimensional mapping.** Only the LIDAR's horizontal scan plane
  is recorded. Adding a servo or tilt mechanism is a separate research
  project and is not on the roadmap.
* **Inter-session loop closure.** slam_toolbox performs loop closure
  within a session, but two scans of the same room taken minutes apart
  do not automatically merge. Export-and-merge across sessions is a
  manual workflow.
* **Autonomous navigation.** There are no motors, no controller, no
  trajectory planner, no `nav2`. The device is carried by a human.
* **Cloud synchronisation.** Maps live on the Pi's PostgreSQL container.
  The user is responsible for backing them up or exporting them.
* **Authentication on the web UI.** The UI is designed for operation on
  an isolated WiFi access point (SSID `Recon`, WPA2). Exposing it on a
  shared LAN without first adding basic authentication is unsafe.
* **Real-time guarantees.** Despite the use of C++17 for hardware-path
  nodes (`sim_sensor_node`, `draw_node`), the system runs on a
  non-realtime Linux kernel and does not claim deterministic latency.
  The 100 Hz IMU rate and 5–10 Hz LIDAR scan rate are soft real-time
  guarantees enforced by the ESP32's cooperative scheduler on one side
  and the Pi's USB-CDC + DDS middleware on the other; jitter is not
  bounded by the design.

## Chapter 2: Hardware Architecture

### 2.1 System-level block diagram

The physical components and their interconnections are best appreciated
through an ASCII block diagram (the canonical form lives in
`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §1):

```
   ┌──────────┐                 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  LD14P   │  Vcc + GND ◄── S8050 (low-side, gated by ESP32 GPIO 4)     │
   │  LIDAR   │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ (4 wire) │  TX (white) ──► ESP32 Serial2 RX (GPIO 16) @ 230 400 8N1   │
   └──────────┘                                                            │
                ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │                       ESP32 DevKit V1                     │
                │  • MPU-6050 @ 100 Hz over I²C 0x68                         │
                │  • 3 buttons (SHUTDOWN/RESET/SAVE) on GPIO 25/26/27         │
                │  • LD14P UART relay (Serial2 → USB-CDC LIDAR_FRAME chunks)  │
                │  • LIDAR_EN (GPIO 4) — 3 s watchdog on Pi refresh          │
                │  • USB-CDC link to Pi @ 460 800 8N1  ───────────────────┐ │
                └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│ │
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴┴─┴─┐
   │                            Raspberry Pi 5                                 │
   │                       Ubuntu 24.04 · ROS2 Jazzy                            │
   │  /dev/ttyUSB0  ─►  esp32_uart_bridge ─► /imu/data_raw  /buttons/*          │
   │                                       /esp32/diagnostics                  │
   │                                       /lidar_enable (service)             │
   │                                       LIDAR bytes ► pty ► /tmp/lidar_pty  │
   │                                                                            │
   │  /tmp/lidar_pty  ─►  ldlidar_stl_ros2_node ─► /scan                        │
   │                                            │                              │
   │                                            ▼                              │
   │                                       slam_toolbox  ─► /map, /tf          │
   │                                                                            │
   │  /imu/data_raw  ─► imu_yaw_integrator ─► /imu/data ─► ekf_node ─► /odom    │
   │                                                                            │
   │  recon_webui_bridge (rclpy on real OS thread)  ─►  Flask + SocketIO :80    │
   │                                            │                              │
   │                                            ▼                              │
   │                                       db_node  ─►  PostgreSQL (Docker)     │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                              │ ap0 10.0.0.1
                                              ▼
                                          ┌────────────────────┐
                                          │  Browser           │
                                          │  http://recon.local │
                                          └────────────────────┘
```

The crucial architectural observation is that **all sensor data
reaches the Pi through a single USB-Serial link**. Even the LIDAR's
high-bandwidth scan packets, which historically connected to the Pi's
PL011 UART (`/dev/ttyAMA0`), now travel through the ESP32 as
`LIDAR_FRAME` envelopes inside the same binary framing protocol that
carries IMU samples and button events. This unification reduces the
number of cables, electrical interfaces, and serial-port permission
issues that the Pi has to manage, at the cost of one extra serial hop
of latency and the throughput overhead of the framing protocol.

### 2.2 Raspberry Pi 5 — role, OS, kernel configuration

The compute platform is a Raspberry Pi 5 with either 4 GB or 8 GB of
RAM. Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (ARM64) is the supported operating
system; the development device runs kernel 6.8.0-1051-raspi. The Pi
runs everything: SLAM, sensor fusion, the web server, the PostgreSQL
container, and the WiFi access point. There is no separate compute
node off-board.

`environment.sh` Section 2 documents the kernel configuration required
to free the Pi's UART resources for use by hardware peripherals.
Although the post-pivot data path does not actually use the Pi's PL011
UART for the LIDAR, the configuration is preserved so that the
`sensor-test --no-esp32` fallback (which re-routes the LIDAR pigtail
directly to the Pi) continues to work when the ESP32 is absent. The
configuration consists of:

1. Three lines appended (idempotently, guarded by `grep`) to
   `/boot/firmware/config.txt`:
   * `enable_uart=1` — enables the UART hardware block.
   * `dtoverlay=uart0` — exposes UART0 as `/dev/ttyAMA0`.
   * `dtoverlay=miniuart-bt` — moves the Bluetooth controller to the
     mini-UART so PL011 (`ttyAMA0`) is dedicated to a peripheral rather
     than to BT.
2. Removal of `console=serial0,...` from `/boot/firmware/cmdline.txt`
   so the kernel does not emit boot messages on the same UART line.
3. `systemctl mask serial-getty@ttyAMA0.service` so no login getty
   binds the device at runtime.
4. A udev rule at `/etc/udev/rules.d/99-lidar-uart.rules` setting the
   group of `/dev/ttyAMA0` to `dialout` and the mode to `0660` so the
   `gabi` user (added to the `dialout` group earlier in the script) can
   open the device without root.
5. The `gabi` user is added to the `dialout` group via `usermod -aG`.

A second capability layer is installed for the web server. Because the
default Flask host port is 80 (a privileged port < 1024), `setcap
cap_net_bind_service=ep /usr/bin/python3.12` is applied. A documented
gotcha (`environment.sh` Section 6, comment) is that **Linux
capabilities cause the dynamic linker to ignore `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`**, so
the ROS2 shared libraries (`librcl_action.so` etc.) under
`/opt/ros/jazzy/lib` must be registered through `ldconfig` rather than
through environment variables. This is done by writing
`/etc/ld.so.conf.d/ros2-jazzy.conf` with the two ROS2 library paths and
running `ldconfig`.

A further documented hazard is that `apt upgrade` of the
`python3.12` package strips the capability on every package update.
`setup.sh` preflight detects this by running `getcap` on the resolved
`python3` binary and, if the capability is missing, exporting
`WEBUI_PORT=8080` with a warning. The web UI then degrades gracefully
to a non-privileged port rather than crashing with `PermissionError:
[Errno 13]`. `REMAINING_ISSUES.md` L13 captures the issue and the
restoration procedure (re-run `environment.sh`).

### 2.3 ESP32 DevKit V1 — role as I/O coprocessor

The ESP32 is an **ESP32-D (WROOM-32 module)** sourced as a DevKit V1
breakout board. Its role is unified into "any peripheral that needs to
talk to the Pi": at present this comprises the MPU-6050 IMU (over I²C),
three momentary push buttons (on GPIO with internal pull-ups), and the
LD14P LIDAR (whose UART output is read on Serial2 and whose power line
is gated by GPIO 4 via an S8050 transistor). The ESP32 is also
positioned to host future SPI peripherals (e.g. a status LED or a
display) without rewiring the Pi.

The ESP32 connects to the Pi via its on-board USB-Serial bridge chip
— either a CP2102 (which enumerates as `/dev/ttyUSB0`) or a CH340
(`/dev/ttyUSB0` on most boards, occasionally `/dev/ttyACM0` on S3/C3
variants with native USB-OTG). The bridge baud is **460 800** since
firmware increment 1 (`firmware/esp32/src/config.h:57`). The previous
115 200 baud was sufficient for IMU-only traffic (~3 KB/s) but is
narrower than the LD14P's native ~23 KB/s data stream and would have
been a bottleneck once Increment 2 added the LIDAR relay path.

Power is taken from the Pi USB port; the ESP32's on-board 3.3 V LDO
regulates the I²C bus voltage for the MPU-6050, and the 5 V VIN rail is
shared with the LD14P. The total combined current draw (Pi 5 + ESP32 +
LIDAR) sits comfortably within the 500 mA per-port USB budget when the
LIDAR motor is running.

### 2.4 LD14P (LD-D200) LIDAR sensor

The LIDAR is a Shenzhen LDROBOT **LD14P (LD-D200)** — a 360° single-line
laser scanner whose firmware-level protocol is shared with the LD19
(hence the `product_name: LDLiDAR_LD19` parameter in
`ld14p.launch.py:26`). Operating characteristics:

| Property              | Value                                             |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Beam type             | Single horizontal line, 360° rotation             |
| Range                 | 0.02 – 8.0 m (LD14P), 25 m advertised in the driver |
| Rotation rate         | 5 – 10 Hz nominal (motor-speed-dependent)         |
| Angular resolution    | ~0.55° nominal, variable with motor speed         |
| UART protocol         | 230 400 baud, 8N1                                 |
| Operating voltage     | 5 V (motor + logic), 3.3 V CMOS UART output       |

#### Electrical interface and the non-standard wire colour issue

The LD14P pigtail is a 4-wire JST connector. The documented wire-to-
function mapping is **non-standard**: it does *not* match the colour
convention (black=GND, red=VCC) used in most hobby and industrial
serial pigtails. A note in `docs/SPEC.md` §2.2 records that the project
originally had Red and Green swapped between two earlier doc revisions
before the correct mapping was confirmed by datasheet on 2026-05-23.
The correct mapping verified against the live hardware is:

| LD14P wire | Function    | Connects to                                                      |
| ---------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Black      | VCC (5 V)   | ESP32 5V (VIN) rail                                              |
| White      | TX (data)   | ESP32 GPIO 16 (Serial2 RX) — 3.3 V CMOS, no level-shifter needed |
| Green      | RX          | S8050 collector (also tied to Red) — "pull to ground for default speed" |
| Red        | GND         | S8050 collector                                                  |

The Green wire on the LD14P is the LIDAR's *receive* line, used by the
sensor to receive optional speed-control commands. With Green tied to
LIDAR-local GND through the S8050 the sensor operates at its default
rotation speed. The Red wire is the LIDAR's ground return. Both wires
terminate at the S8050 collector simultaneously because allowing only
GND to be switched while RX floats at 3.3 V (via an internal pull-up
inside the LIDAR) would phantom-power the device when the transistor
was open, and the LIDAR would continue spinning at low torque.

This **non-standard wire colour issue** is a documented project
gotcha (`STATUS.md` §7 #14 in the pre-pivot archive; `SPEC.md` §2.2 in
the current document) and is the single highest-value piece of
"undocumented knowledge" the project preserves: anyone re-wiring the
LD14P pigtail from scratch is overwhelmingly likely to assume standard
colour conventions and either fail to bring the sensor up (Black-to-GND
short on the 5 V rail) or worse, damage it.

### 2.5 MPU-6050 IMU — register-level configuration

The inertial measurement unit is an **InvenSense MPU-6050**, a 6-axis
chip combining a 3-axis accelerometer and a 3-axis gyroscope on a
single die. It exposes an I²C interface at address `0x68` (AD0 tied to
GND) and is wired to the ESP32 at the standard DevKit V1 I²C pins
(GPIO 21 SDA, GPIO 22 SCL, 3.3 V VCC). The bus runs at I²C fast mode,
400 kHz.

The firmware initialisation sequence (`firmware/esp32/src/imu.cpp`
function `begin()`) is structured to be defensive against the
documented power-on quirks of the chip:

1. **Bus initialisation.** `Wire.begin(PIN_I2C_SDA, PIN_I2C_SCL,
   I2C_FREQ_HZ)` configures the I²C controller; `Wire.setTimeOut(50)`
   bounds bus stalls to 50 ms so a wedged peripheral cannot block the
   firmware loop.
2. **WHO_AM_I check.** Register `0x75` is read and verified to be
   `0x68` (genuine MPU-6050), `0x70` (some clones) or `0x72` (other
   clones). A mismatch fails `begin()` cleanly.
3. **Device reset.** Bit 7 (`DEVICE_RESET`) of `PWR_MGMT_1` (`0x6B`) is
   set high, and a 100 ms delay is inserted. The datasheet quotes
   30–35 ms for "stable IMU operation" after reset; 100 ms is
   comfortable headroom. The firmware comment notes a documented
   failure mode: range-configuration writes made too soon after
   power-on are silently dropped, and the accelerometer stays at its
   default ±2 g range. The symptom is that gravity reads twice the
   expected value (about 19.6 m/s² instead of 9.8) — almost
   indistinguishable from the factory `ZA_OFFSET` bias issue, so the
   reset-and-wait pattern is essential.
4. **Wake from sleep, set clock source.** `PWR_MGMT_1` is written
   `0x01`, which wakes the device (clears `SLEEP`) and selects the
   X-axis gyro PLL as the clock source (`CLKSEL = 1`). A 50 ms delay
   follows.
5. **Sample rate divider.** `SMPLRT_DIV` (`0x19`) is set to `9`. With
   the on-chip digital low-pass filter active (`CONFIG ≠ 0` and `≠ 7`)
   the gyro output rate is 1 kHz, so the output sample rate becomes
   1000 / (1 + 9) = **100 Hz**.
6. **Low-pass filter cutoff.** `CONFIG` (`0x1A`) is set to `0x03`,
   which selects approximately 44 Hz accelerometer cutoff and 42 Hz
   gyro cutoff. This bandwidth comfortably exceeds the 10 Hz expected
   bandwidth of human hand motion while attenuating high-frequency
   mechanical vibration noise.
7. **Gyro full-scale.** `GYRO_CONFIG` (`0x1B`) is set to `0x08`, which
   selects ±500 °/s (`FS_SEL = 1`). The corresponding sensitivity is
   65.5 LSB per °/s.
8. **Accelerometer full-scale.** `ACCEL_CONFIG` (`0x1C`) is set to
   `0x08`, which selects ±4 g (`AFS_SEL = 1`). The corresponding
   sensitivity is 8192 LSB per g.
9. **Range verification.** Both `GYRO_CONFIG` and `ACCEL_CONFIG` are
   read back; if bits `[4:3]` are not the expected `0x08` mask the
   `begin()` returns failure. This catches the silently-dropped-write
   pathology described above.
10. **ZA_OFFSET diagnostic capture.** `ZA_OFFSET_H` and `ZA_OFFSET_L`
    (`0x0A`/`0x0B`) are read but *not modified*. The factory ZA_OFFSET
    on the bench unit measured 1544 LSB and biases the accelerometer Z
    reading by ~5.5 m/s², so a stationary chip reads about 15.3 m/s²
    on the Z axis instead of the expected 9.8. The firmware records
    both `before` and `after` values (identical, because no write
    happens) and ships them in the boot STATUS frame so the Pi-side
    decoder can display the chip's factory bias.

A **hard-won lesson** appears as a 19-line comment in `imu.cpp` around
the ZA_OFFSET capture (lines 126–138). Naively writing 0 to
`ZA_OFFSET_L` clobbers a reserved temperature-compensation gate in
bit 0 and **worsens** the bias rather than fixing it. The bench
measurement quoted in the comment is "gravity total magnitude measured
7.83 m/s² after a naive zero-write vs 15.35 with the factory bias
intact". The chip's reading is therefore left exactly as the factory
trimmed it, and the EKF (Chapter 6) handles online bias removal.

Conversion from the chip's raw 16-bit signed counts to SI units happens
on the ESP32, not on the Pi:

```cpp
ACCEL_LSB_TO_MS2  = 9.80665f / 8192.0f      // ≈ 1.197e-3 m/s² per LSB
GYRO_LSB_TO_RADS  = (PI / 180.0f) / 65.5f   // ≈ 2.661e-4 rad/s per LSB
```

The conversion is intentionally performed before the data leaves the
microcontroller because the wire format ships SI floats anyway (six
`float32` values per IMU frame); doing the conversion at the source
keeps the Pi-side parsing trivial.

Sample reads (`imu::read()`) request a 14-byte burst starting at
`ACCEL_XOUT_H` (`0x3B`). The 14 bytes encode `AX_H AX_L AY_H AY_L AZ_H
AZ_L T_H T_L GX_H GX_L GY_H GY_L GZ_H GZ_L`. The temperature bytes are
read and discarded — temperature compensation is not exposed in the
data path. The six 16-bit signed values are reconstructed by shifting
the high byte and ORing the low byte, multiplied by the LSB-to-SI
factors, and written into the output `ImuSample` struct.

### 2.6 S8050 NPN transistor motor-gate circuit

The S8050 is a small-signal NPN bipolar junction transistor in TO-92
package, rated for 25 V Vce and 500 mA continuous collector current.
The Recon-Platform-R2 schematic places it as a **low-side switch** on
the LD14P's combined GND-and-RX rail:

```
ESP32 GPIO 4 ──[ 1 kΩ ]── S8050 base
ESP32 GND   ────────────── S8050 emitter
LD14P Red + Green ──────── S8050 collector
LD14P Black ─────────────── ESP32 5V (VIN)
LD14P White ─────────────── ESP32 GPIO 16 (Serial2 RX)
```

When ESP32 GPIO 4 (`PIN_LIDAR_EN` in `firmware/esp32/src/config.h:33`)
is driven HIGH at 3.3 V, the base-emitter junction is forward-biased
and the transistor saturates. The collector is pulled to within ~200
mV of emitter (i.e. essentially ground), and the LIDAR's combined
GND/RX path completes through it. The LIDAR powers up and begins
spinning. When GPIO 4 is LOW, the transistor is cut off, no current
flows through the collector, and the LIDAR has no ground return —
which is functionally equivalent to disconnecting its power.

#### Why low-side switching?

Two reasons:

1. **Driver simplicity.** A high-side switch (PMOS or PNP) would
   require the LD14P 5 V rail to be switched. The S8050 NPN low-side
   switch is driven directly from a 3.3 V GPIO with no level-shifting,
   and the 1 kΩ base resistor is the only passive component required.
2. **Failure mode preference.** With the transistor open, the LIDAR
   is floating-ground. If the ESP32 is unpowered, GPIO 4 is at a true
   high-impedance state, the base is pulled to ground via the resistor
   and the transistor stays off. The LIDAR fails *safe* (motor off)
   under loss-of-control conditions.

The `firmware/esp32/src/main.cpp:setup()` function explicitly drives
`PIN_LIDAR_EN` LOW as **the first executable instruction** in
`setup()`, before any `Serial.begin()` or peripheral initialisation:

```cpp
void setup() {
    // FAIL-SAFE FIRST: motor stays off through the boot window. ...
    pinMode(PIN_LIDAR_EN, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(PIN_LIDAR_EN, LOW);
    g_lidar_enabled = false;
    ...
}
```

This ordering matters because the ESP32 takes approximately 200 ms to
finish its bootloader sequence and enter `setup()`. During that window
GPIO 4 is in its default state (input, high-impedance). If the LIDAR
were powered from a rail that the GPIO actively controlled, this
high-impedance period could be enough for the motor to start spinning
before the firmware was ready to control it. By making GPIO 4 an output
and driving it LOW first, the firmware closes that window to the
minimum possible (a few clock cycles between `pinMode` and
`digitalWrite`). An external pull-down resistor on the base would
achieve the same effect but at the cost of an extra component.

A 3-second software **watchdog** in the firmware closes a related hole.
While the LIDAR is enabled, the Pi-side bridge re-sends `LIDAR_EN=1`
every 1 second (see `recon_hardware/esp32_uart_bridge.py:_refresh_lidar`).
If three seconds pass without a refresh frame, the firmware
unconditionally drives `PIN_LIDAR_EN` LOW. The intent is to prevent the
LIDAR from spinning indefinitely after a Pi crash or USB disconnect —
the user might unplug the device and walk away assuming it has shut
down, but if the firmware did not enforce a watchdog, the motor would
continue spinning. The watchdog timeout (`LIDAR_WATCHDOG_MS = 3000`)
is comfortably larger than the refresh interval (1000 ms) to absorb
transient delays without false trips.

A subtle bug fix is documented in the watchdog comparison. The naïve
implementation `(now - last_refresh_ms) > LIDAR_WATCHDOG_MS` performs
unsigned 32-bit subtraction; if `last_refresh_ms` was set slightly
later than `now` by a concurrent code path (e.g. a refresh frame
arrived during the same loop iteration, between the `now = millis()`
read and the watchdog comparison), the subtraction underflows to a
huge positive number and the watchdog trips. The firmware uses
**signed** `(int32_t)` casts on every `millis()`-based comparison:

```cpp
if (g_lidar_enabled &&
    (int32_t)(now - g_lidar_last_refresh_ms) > (int32_t)LIDAR_WATCHDOG_MS) {
    set_lidar_enabled(false);
}
```

The signed difference correctly evaluates to a small negative number
when `last_refresh_ms > now`, the comparison fails, and the watchdog
does not trip. This pattern is applied to all four `millis()`-based
deadlines in `loop()` (IMU sample, heartbeat, LED toggle, watchdog).
The fix is enshrined as a binding rule in `docs/AGENT_RULES.md` §10
("Signed `(int32_t)` math for every `millis()`-based comparison").

### 2.7 Button debounce hardware vs software responsibility split

Three momentary push-buttons are connected to GPIO 25, 26 and 27 on the
ESP32 (`PIN_BTN_SHUTDOWN`, `PIN_BTN_STARTSTOP`, `PIN_BTN_SAVE` in
`config.h:21-23`). They are wired one terminal to GPIO, one terminal to
ground. The internal pull-up resistor inside the ESP32's GPIO pad
provides the rest-state high. Pressing a button shorts the GPIO to
ground and the firmware sees `digitalRead == LOW`.

Crucially, **no hardware debouncing is provided**. There is no RC
filter, no Schmitt trigger, no dedicated debouncer chip. The bounce
behaviour of a mechanical switch contact closure produces a burst of
spurious `HIGH ↔ LOW` transitions over the first few milliseconds of
contact; without filtering this would generate dozens of phantom
`PRESSED` events per real press.

The firmware (`firmware/esp32/src/buttons.cpp`) implements a
**standard wait-for-stability** debounce in software:

1. Each iteration of `Button::update`, the raw GPIO is read.
2. If the raw read differs from the **last raw** read, the timestamp
   is recorded and no event is emitted (this handles a transition that
   has just begun).
3. If the raw read differs from the **stable** state AND
   `BUTTON_DEBOUNCE_MS` (25 ms, from `config.h:69`) have elapsed since
   the last raw change, the stable state is updated and a
   `PRESSED` or `RELEASED` edge event is emitted.
4. If the button is stable-pressed AND `BUTTON_LONGPRESS_MS` (2 s,
   from `config.h:70`) have elapsed since the press began AND no
   long-press event has already fired for this press, a `LONGPRESS`
   event is emitted.

The 25 ms debounce window is comfortably longer than typical contact
bounce (which usually settles within 1–5 ms) but short enough that the
user does not perceive a press lag. The state machine is encapsulated
in a `Button` class that takes a callback function pointer; the
callback is invoked at most once per `update` call with the button id
and the new state.

The **responsibility split** between hardware and software is therefore
"hardware provides nothing, software provides everything". This is a
deliberate cost-minimisation choice: any external debouncer adds bill
of materials, board area and assembly time, and a 25 ms software
window achieves indistinguishable results in this application's
control loop.

### 2.8 Power budget

The whole device runs from a single **22.5 W USB-C power bank** plugged
into the Pi 5's USB-C input. The Pi powers the ESP32 from one of its USB
ports, and the LD14P shares the ESP32's VIN (5 V) rail through the JST
connector. One source feeds everything; there is no separate buck
converter or battery-rail wiring to get wrong on the high-current side.

The power bank's own button is the hard on/off. The SHUTDOWN button on
the ESP32 is a *signal* only (it generates a button event that the bridge
forwards to ROS2, which `db_node` or a future `shutdown_handler` node will
convert into `sudo shutdown -h now`); actually cutting power means
switching the power bank off or unplugging the USB-C cable. This
separation gives the operator a clear escape: if the firmware hangs and
stops processing button events, the power bank button still works.

A USB current budget summary:

| Consumer            | Typical current at 5 V |
| ------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Pi 5 (idle + WiFi)  | 600 – 800 mA            |
| Pi 5 (under load)   | 1.0 – 1.5 A              |
| ESP32 + LD14P motor | 200 – 350 mA (motor on) |
| ESP32 (motor off)   | < 50 mA                  |

When the LIDAR motor is on, the total system draw is approximately
1.5–2.0 A at 5 V — well within the **22.5 W USB-C power bank**'s output
envelope. Mechanical mounting of the bank inside the enclosure is
deferred to stage H6 of the roadmap.

A reconciliation between the three sources of truth for the ESP32
pinout is given below. Where a row is consistent across all three
sources, the entry is marked **OK**.

| Function           | `docs/SPEC.md` §2.3 | `firmware/esp32/src/config.h` | `firmware/esp32/src/main.cpp` | Cross-check |
| ------------------ | ------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------- |
| MPU-6050 SDA       | GPIO 21             | `PIN_I2C_SDA = 21`            | (Wire.begin uses config)      | OK          |
| MPU-6050 SCL       | GPIO 22             | `PIN_I2C_SCL = 22`            | (Wire.begin uses config)      | OK          |
| Button SHUTDOWN    | GPIO 25             | `PIN_BTN_SHUTDOWN = 25`       | `g_btn_shutdown.begin(BTN_SHUTDOWN, PIN_BTN_SHUTDOWN)` | OK |
| Button START/STOP       | GPIO 26             | `PIN_BTN_STARTSTOP = 26`          | similarly                     | OK          |
| Button SAVE        | GPIO 27             | `PIN_BTN_SAVE = 27`           | similarly                     | OK          |
| Status LED         | GPIO 2              | `PIN_STATUS_LED = 2`          | `digitalWrite(PIN_STATUS_LED, …)` | OK    |
| LIDAR enable       | GPIO 4              | `PIN_LIDAR_EN = 4`            | `pinMode(PIN_LIDAR_EN, OUTPUT)` first line of `setup()` | OK |
| LIDAR Serial2 RX   | GPIO 16             | `PIN_LIDAR_SERIAL2_RX = 16`   | `Serial2.begin(LIDAR_SERIAL2_BAUD, SERIAL_8N1, PIN_LIDAR_SERIAL2_RX, -1)` | OK |
| USB-CDC baud (Pi)  | 460 800             | `UART_BAUD = 460800`          | `Serial.begin(UART_BAUD)`      | OK          |
| LIDAR baud         | 230 400             | `LIDAR_SERIAL2_BAUD = 230400` | (used in `Serial2.begin`)      | OK          |

No discrepancies are present in the pinout assignments. This is a
direct consequence of `AGENT_RULES.md` §3 ("Config over constants —
ESP32 pinout lives in `firmware/esp32/src/config.h`; pinout for the
LIDAR lives in `roomba_ws/config/hardware.yaml`").

**[DISCREPANCY: docs/SPEC.md §2.2 wiring table — Pi-side]**:
`roomba_ws/config/hardware.yaml` still declares the LIDAR `serial_port:
"/dev/ttyAMA0"` and `baud_rate: 230400`. These values are vestigial
from the pre-pivot direct-UART configuration and are **not loaded** by
any node in the current setup (the `ldlidar_stl_ros2` driver is
launched with explicit parameters in `ld14p.launch.py`, which sets
`port_name: '/tmp/lidar_pty'`). `hardware.yaml` is therefore
documentation-only as far as the LIDAR is concerned; the doc string in
`docs/SPEC.md` §7 acknowledges it is "LIDAR-only static doc". This is
not a functional bug but is a latent trap: a future developer reading
`hardware.yaml` may assume the listed values are authoritative when in
fact the pty path overrides them.

## Chapter 3: ESP32 Firmware

### 3.1 Build system: PlatformIO, arduino-esp32 framework, flash/RAM usage

The ESP32 firmware lives in `firmware/esp32/` and is built with
**PlatformIO Core**. The project configuration in `platformio.ini`
declares a single environment `[env:esp32dev]` targeting the
`espressif32` platform with `board = esp32dev` (generic 4 MB flash
DevKit V1) and `framework = arduino`. Compiler flags select C++17
(`-std=gnu++17`), enable `-Wall -Wextra`, and suppress the unused-
parameter warning that the Arduino core's `Wire.h` triggers on some
toolchains.

The serial monitor speed in `platformio.ini` is left at `monitor_speed
= 115200` (the legacy Arduino default), while `upload_speed` is bumped
to 921 600 baud to halve the flash time on large binaries. Both values
are decoupled from the wire-format baud in `config.h` so neither has
to track changes in the runtime UART configuration.

The `firmware/esp32/environment.sh` provisioner reports a typical
build size of approximately **22% flash usage** on a 4 MB partition,
leaving substantial room for future opcodes or peripherals. RAM usage
is dominated by the 1 KB `Serial2.setRxBufferSize(1024)` buffer
(`main.cpp:101`) plus the framing scope buffer (`2 + MAX_PAYLOAD = 66`
bytes per frame send) and is comfortably below the WROOM-32's 520 KB
DRAM budget.

No external libraries beyond the framework are used. Per
`AGENT_RULES.md` §10 ("No external libraries beyond the framework"),
the firmware compiles against only `Arduino.h` and `Wire.h`. The
project preference is to own the I²C reads rather than depend on
`Adafruit_MPU6050` or similar — the trade-off is a few hundred
additional lines of code in exchange for full control over reset
sequencing, range verification, and the careful avoidance of
ZA_OFFSET writes documented in §2.5.

### 3.2 `config.h` — every constant explained

`firmware/esp32/src/config.h` is the canonical pinout-and-tunables
header for the entire firmware. Every other source file includes it.
The 100-odd lines of the file are organised in commented sections:

* **I²C (MPU-6050).** `PIN_I2C_SDA = 21`, `PIN_I2C_SCL = 22`,
  `I2C_FREQ_HZ = 400000` (I²C fast mode), `MPU6050_ADDR = 0x68` (AD0
  tied LOW).
* **Buttons.** `PIN_BTN_SHUTDOWN = 25`, `PIN_BTN_STARTSTOP = 26`,
  `PIN_BTN_SAVE = 27`.
* **Status LED.** `PIN_STATUS_LED = 2` (onboard blue LED on most
  DevKit V1 boards).
* **LIDAR power control.** `PIN_LIDAR_EN = 4` (drives S8050 base
  through 1 kΩ); `LIDAR_WATCHDOG_MS = 3000` (firmware timeout if Pi
  stops refreshing the enable line).
* **LIDAR data ingestion.** `PIN_LIDAR_SERIAL2_RX = 16` (ESP32
  Serial2 RX); `LIDAR_SERIAL2_BAUD = 230400` (LD14P native baud).
* **USB-Serial uplink to the Pi.** `UART_BAUD = 460800`. A long
  comment explains the choice: 115 200 was sufficient for IMU-only
  traffic but cannot carry 23 KB/s of LIDAR data on top of 3 KB/s
  IMU plus framing overhead. 460 800 8N1 has ~46 KB/s of sustained
  budget, comfortably over the measured 26 KB/s steady-state.
* **Loop schedule.** `IMU_RATE_HZ = 100`,
  `IMU_PERIOD_MS = 1000 / IMU_RATE_HZ` (= 10 ms),
  `HEARTBEAT_PERIOD_MS = 1000`,
  `BUTTON_DEBOUNCE_MS = 25`, `BUTTON_LONGPRESS_MS = 2000`.
* **UART framing.** `SYNC_BYTE_0 = 0xA5`, `SYNC_BYTE_1 = 0x5A`. The
  pattern was chosen to be unlikely in IMU float streams (no
  representable IEEE-754 single-precision value produces the
  consecutive byte sequence `0xA5 0x5A` in either endianness for any
  reasonable physical magnitude).
* **Frame type enum** (`FrameType`). Values 0x01..0x07: `FRAME_IMU`,
  `FRAME_BUTTON`, `FRAME_HEARTBEAT`, `FRAME_STATUS`,
  `FRAME_LIDAR_FRAME`, `FRAME_LIDAR_EN`, `FRAME_LIDAR_ACK`. The
  enumeration is canonical and mirrored byte-for-byte in
  `recon_hardware/framing.py` on the Pi side.
* **Button identity enum** (`ButtonId`). `BTN_SHUTDOWN=0`,
  `BTN_STARTSTOP=1`, `BTN_SAVE=2`.
* **Button state enum** (`ButtonState`). `BTN_RELEASED=0`,
  `BTN_PRESSED=1`, `BTN_LONGPRESS=2`.
* **STATUS flag bitmask.** `STATUS_BOOT = 1 << 0` (set on first frame
  after boot), `STATUS_IMU_OK = 1 << 1` (0 ⇒ IMU not responding on
  I²C), `STATUS_IMU_DATA = 1 << 2` (1 ⇒ first valid sample seen).

There are no magic numbers in any other source file. Each integer
constant in the firmware traces back to one of the names declared in
`config.h`, ensuring that a single edit-and-reflash propagates a
configuration change. This is `AGENT_RULES.md` §3 ("Config over
constants") enforced at the lowest level of the system.

### 3.3 Cooperative scheduler pattern in `main.cpp`

The firmware runs no FreeRTOS tasks — the Arduino main loop drives
everything cooperatively. The structure of `loop()` (`main.cpp:125-195`)
is a sequence of `millis()`-deadline-gated work items, each guarded by
a signed comparison against the captured `now` timestamp:

```cpp
void loop() {
    const uint32_t now = millis();

    // 1. Drain incoming frames from Pi (LIDAR_EN, future opcodes).
    while (Serial.available() > 0) {
        framing::ParsedFrame f;
        const int b = Serial.read();
        if (b >= 0 && g_pi_parser.feed((uint8_t)b, f)) {
            handle_incoming_frame(f);
        }
    }

    // 2. LIDAR data relay: drain Serial2 RX into a LIDAR_FRAME envelope.
    if (g_lidar_enabled) {
        const int avail = Serial2.available();
        if (avail > 0) {
            uint8_t buf[framing::MAX_PAYLOAD];
            const int to_read = (avail > (int)sizeof(buf))
                                ? (int)sizeof(buf) : avail;
            const int got = Serial2.readBytes(buf, to_read);
            if (got > 0) framing::send_lidar_frame(buf, (uint8_t)got);
        }
    }

    // 3. LIDAR watchdog: signed comparison to avoid underflow.
    if (g_lidar_enabled &&
        (int32_t)(now - g_lidar_last_refresh_ms) > (int32_t)LIDAR_WATCHDOG_MS) {
        set_lidar_enabled(false);
    }

    // 4. Button polling (each Button::update is bounded and non-blocking).
    g_btn_shutdown.update(on_button_event);
    g_btn_startstop.update   (on_button_event);
    g_btn_save.update    (on_button_event);

    // 5. IMU sample at IMU_RATE_HZ.
    if ((int32_t)(now - g_next_imu_ms) >= 0) {
        g_next_imu_ms += IMU_PERIOD_MS;
        ImuSample s;
        if (imu::read(s)) {
            framing::send_imu(s.ax, s.ay, s.az, s.gx, s.gy, s.gz);
        } else {
            (void)imu::begin();   // attempt bus recovery
            framing::send_status(imu::ok() ? STATUS_IMU_OK : 0);
        }
    }

    // 6. Heartbeat.
    if ((int32_t)(now - g_next_heartbeat_ms) >= 0) {
        g_next_heartbeat_ms += HEARTBEAT_PERIOD_MS;
        framing::send_heartbeat(now);
    }

    // 7. Status LED.
    update_status_led();
}
```

#### Timing guarantees and their limits

The loop body runs at approximately 1 kHz on the ESP32 (the
measurements documented in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §7 quote ">1 kHz"
for the bench device). At 1 kHz iteration rate:

* **IMU sampling is on-time to ~1 ms.** The 10 ms IMU deadline is
  guaranteed to be met within one loop iteration of the scheduled
  time, so jitter is bounded by the iteration period.
* **Button debounce sees fresh state at ~1 ms.** With a 25 ms
  debounce window the effective edge resolution is the maximum of
  the iteration period (~1 ms) and the GPIO-read latency, which is a
  handful of microseconds.
* **LIDAR relay throughput.** One chunk of up to 64 bytes per
  iteration ⇒ 64 KB/s achievable, comfortably over the LD14P's
  ~23 KB/s peak. The `Serial2.setRxBufferSize(1024)` call ensures
  that a transient stall of up to ~45 ms can be absorbed before the
  hardware FIFO overflows.

The scheduler's main weakness is that **any one item that blocks for
more than ~10 ms will cause IMU sample loss**. The longest realistic
blocking call is `imu::begin()` after an I²C failure (which includes
a 100 ms `delay()` for `DEVICE_RESET`). The firmware accepts this
trade-off because IMU re-init is rare and the recovery path is
explicit; ordinary loop iterations do not invoke any blocking I/O.

The decision *not* to use FreeRTOS tasks is documented in
`AGENT_RULES.md` §10 ("Cooperative scheduling. No FreeRTOS tasks for
the current workload"). The justification is workload simplicity: with
only one high-rate producer (the 100 Hz IMU) and one bursty I/O
channel (the LIDAR relay), the additional context-switch overhead and
priority-inversion risk of FreeRTOS multitasking outweighs the value.
Should a higher-rate sensor (e.g. a 1 kHz IMU or an audio input)
appear in a future revision, the loop will need to be refactored.

### 3.4 `framing.h` / `framing.cpp` — binary frame format byte-by-byte

The wire format is identical to the canonical specification in
`docs/UART_PROTOCOL.md` §2:

```
  0       1       2       3       4..4+LEN-1     4+LEN
  ┌───────┬───────┬───────┬───────┬─────────────┬───────┐
  │ 0xA5  │ 0x5A  │ TYPE  │ LEN   │ PAYLOAD ... │ CRC8  │
  └───────┴───────┴───────┴───────┴─────────────┴───────┘
                             \________ CRC scope ________/
```

* **SYNC[0] / SYNC[1]:** Constants `0xA5 0x5A`. Used by the parser to
  re-synchronise after byte loss. Excluded from CRC.
* **TYPE:** One byte, one of the `FrameType` enum values.
* **LEN:** One byte, payload length in bytes. `0 ≤ LEN ≤ 64`. The
  64-byte ceiling is set by `framing::MAX_PAYLOAD` (`framing.h:27`);
  the upper bound was bumped from the pre-LIDAR ceiling of 24 to 64 in
  Increment 2 to let `LIDAR_FRAME` carry "a couple of LD14P scan
  packets (47 B each) per envelope".
* **PAYLOAD:** `LEN` bytes of type-specific data. Little-endian for
  multi-byte integers and IEEE-754 single-precision floats.
* **CRC8:** One byte, Dallas/Maxim CRC-8 (polynomial `0x07`, init
  `0x00`, no input reflection, no output reflection, no XOR-out). The
  CRC is computed over the `TYPE + LEN + PAYLOAD` scope only — sync
  bytes are excluded so that resync logic can scan for them
  independently of any CRC machinery.

#### Encode path

`framing::send_frame(uint8_t type, const uint8_t* payload, uint8_t len)`
(`framing.cpp:22-41`) is the universal sender. It refuses to send if
`len > MAX_PAYLOAD`. It builds a stack buffer containing
`[TYPE, LEN, PAYLOAD...]`, computes the CRC over that buffer with one
pass through `framing::crc8`, and writes the sync bytes, the scope,
and the CRC to the hardware `Serial`. The hashing-once-then-write
pattern avoids byte-feeding the CRC routine through `Serial.write`
calls and keeps the call to `Serial.write` an atomic single-buffer
transaction.

Six convenience functions wrap `send_frame` for each outgoing frame
type:

| Function                                       | TYPE        | Payload                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `send_imu(ax,ay,az,gx,gy,gz)`                  | `0x01` IMU  | 24 B = 6 × float32 (little-endian via `memcpy`) |
| `send_button(id, state)`                       | `0x02`      | 2 B = `uint8 id`, `uint8 state`               |
| `send_heartbeat(uptime_ms)`                    | `0x03`      | 4 B = `uint32 uptime_ms` (LE)                 |
| `send_status(flags)`                           | `0x04`      | 2 B = `uint8 flags`, `uint8 0` (reserved)     |
| `send_status_diag(flags, who, accel_cfg, gyro_cfg, za_b, za_a)` | `0x04` (extended) | 8 B = boot diagnostic blob |
| `send_lidar_frame(buf, len)`                   | `0x05`      | 1..64 raw LIDAR bytes                         |
| `send_lidar_ack(enabled)`                      | `0x07`      | 1 B = `uint8 enabled`                         |

#### Decode path (incoming Pi → ESP32)

The incoming-frame parser `framing::FrameParser` (`framing.cpp:101-155`)
is a mirror of the Pi-side Python parser in
`recon_hardware/framing.py`. It is a six-state machine: `HUNT0`,
`HUNT1`, `TYPE`, `LEN`, `PAY`, `CRC`. The transitions are:

| State    | Byte received                | Next state   |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ------------ |
| HUNT0    | `0xA5`                       | HUNT1        |
| HUNT0    | anything else                | HUNT0        |
| HUNT1    | `0x5A`                       | TYPE         |
| HUNT1    | `0xA5` (consecutive)         | HUNT1 (stay) |
| HUNT1    | anything else                | HUNT0        |
| TYPE     | any byte                     | LEN          |
| LEN      | `b > MAX_PAYLOAD`            | HUNT0 (drop) |
| LEN      | `b == 0`                     | CRC          |
| LEN      | `0 < b ≤ MAX_PAYLOAD`        | PAY          |
| PAY      | (collect until `fidx == flen`) | CRC        |
| CRC      | valid CRC                    | HUNT0, emit  |
| CRC      | invalid CRC                  | HUNT0, drop  |

The "consecutive `0xA5` in HUNT1" branch is a subtle but important
recovery case. If the previous frame's last byte happened to be
`0xA5`, the parser's `HUNT0` state correctly transitioned to `HUNT1`.
If the next byte is *also* `0xA5` (e.g. an extra `0xA5` is emitted by
the firmware as part of the next frame), naively the state machine
would reject it as "not `0x5A`" and reset to `HUNT0`, missing the real
start of the next frame. The "stay armed" branch keeps the parser in
`HUNT1` so the next `0x5A` is still valid. This is verified by
`tests/test_esp32_uart_bridge.py::test_consecutive_syncs_still_parse`.

Two error counters track parser health:

* `crc_fail_count` — incremented every time CRC validation fails.
* `bad_len_count` — incremented every time the LEN field is greater
  than `MAX_PAYLOAD`. This catches "stray byte interpreted as LEN" —
  for example, the byte sequence `0xA5 0x5A 0x01 0xFF ...` would be
  interpreted as TYPE=1 LEN=255 if not for this guard.

### 3.5 `imu.h` / `imu.cpp` — register-level MPU-6050 driver

Already described in detail in §2.5. The salient implementation
points not already covered:

* **`write_reg(reg, value)`** uses `Wire.beginTransmission` /
  `Wire.write` / `Wire.endTransmission`, returning true iff
  `endTransmission()` returned 0 (ACK received).
* **`read_reg(reg, value)`** uses the "restart" pattern:
  `endTransmission(false)` keeps the bus active so the subsequent
  `requestFrom(addr, 1)` is a repeated-start read rather than a fresh
  transaction.
* **Bus stall timeout.** `Wire.setTimeOut(50)` bounds any single bus
  operation to 50 ms. Without this, a wedged peripheral (e.g. a
  shorted SDA line) would cause an Arduino-core call to block
  indefinitely.
* **`ok()` and `read()` interaction.** `read()` returns false
  immediately if `g_ok` is false, so a failed `begin()` propagates as
  "no IMU data" through the loop's IMU branch, which in turn invokes
  `imu::begin()` again on the next iteration. The retry-on-failure
  pattern is what powers the slow-blink LED diagnostic: as long as
  `begin()` keeps failing, `imu::ok()` stays false, and the
  `update_status_led()` function in `main.cpp` toggles the LED at
  ~1 Hz.

### 3.6 `buttons.h` / `buttons.cpp` — debounce + long-press state machine

Already described in §2.7. The implementation is intentionally
minimal — 60 lines of `.cpp` total. The `Button` class state is:

* `id_` — opaque identifier passed through to the callback.
* `pin_` — the GPIO number.
* `stable_pressed_` — the last debounced state.
* `last_raw_pressed_` — the last raw read.
* `last_change_ms_` — timestamp of the most recent raw-edge.
* `press_start_ms_` — timestamp of the most recent stable PRESSED.
* `longpress_fired_` — flag to ensure long-press fires only once per
  press.

The callback type `void (*on_event)(uint8_t id, uint8_t state)` is a
plain function pointer, deliberately chosen over a `std::function` to
avoid the heap allocation that `std::function` may perform. Three
global `Button` instances are declared in the anonymous namespace of
`main.cpp` and bound to the three button GPIOs in `setup()`; the
shared `on_button_event` callback simply forwards `(id, state)` to
`framing::send_button`.

### 3.7 LIDAR relay path

Already described in §2.4 and §3.3. The relay path comprises:

1. **Serial2 ingest.** `Serial2.setRxBufferSize(1024)` is called
   before `Serial2.begin` (the buffer must be sized before the
   peripheral is started, otherwise the call silently has no effect).
2. **Per-iteration drain.** In `loop()`, if `g_lidar_enabled` is true
   and `Serial2.available() > 0`, up to 64 bytes are read into a
   stack buffer and forwarded as a single `FRAME_LIDAR_FRAME` envelope.
3. **No-power, no-relay invariant.** When `g_lidar_enabled` is false,
   the `Serial2.available()` check is skipped entirely. Any stray
   bytes that the LIDAR may have emitted just before motor-off are
   discarded.

### 3.8 Bidirectional protocol: all seven opcode types

The complete opcode table is reproduced below for thesis reference.
The "Rate" column gives the design rate; the "Trigger" column gives
the producing condition.

| TYPE | Name          | Direction  | LEN   | Rate / trigger        | Payload                                                  |
| ---- | ------------- | ---------- | ----- | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0x01 | IMU           | ESP→Pi     | 24    | 100 Hz                | 6 × float32 `(ax, ay, az / gx, gy, gz)`                  |
| 0x02 | BUTTON        | ESP→Pi     | 2     | edge event            | `uint8 id` (0=SHUTDOWN, 1=START/STOP, 2=SAVE), `uint8 state` (0=RELEASED, 1=PRESSED, 2=LONGPRESS) |
| 0x03 | HEARTBEAT     | ESP→Pi     | 4     | 1 Hz                  | `uint32 uptime_ms` (LE)                                  |
| 0x04 | STATUS        | ESP→Pi     | 2 or 8 | boot + on IMU error  | `uint8 flags, uint8 0` (short variant) or `uint8 flags, uint8 who_am_i, uint8 accel_cfg, uint8 gyro_cfg, int16 za_off_before, int16 za_off_after` (extended boot variant) |
| 0x05 | LIDAR_FRAME   | ESP→Pi     | 1..64 | as bytes arrive       | Raw LD14P UART bytes                                     |
| 0x06 | LIDAR_EN      | Pi→ESP     | 1     | event + 1 Hz refresh  | `uint8 enable` (0=off, 1=on)                             |
| 0x07 | LIDAR_ACK     | ESP→Pi     | 1     | on state change       | `uint8 enabled` (current motor state)                    |

A normal button press generates two frames: `PRESSED` on the falling
edge (after 25 ms debounce), `RELEASED` on the rising edge. A press
held for ≥ 2 000 ms generates an additional `LONGPRESS` frame between
them.

### 3.9 Known firmware limitations and TODOs

The firmware is small and the surface area for unhandled cases is
correspondingly small. The known limitations, drawn from
`REMAINING_ISSUES.md` and source comments:

* **M1: LIDAR_FRAME / LIDAR_EN / LIDAR_ACK lack pytest coverage.** The
  three opcodes added in Increments 1 and 2 are exercised end-to-end
  on hardware but the Pi-side `recon_hardware/framing.py` test suite
  covers only `IMU`/`BUTTON`/`HEARTBEAT`/`STATUS` round-trips.
  Concrete fix outlined in §10.8 below.
* **L4: Boot STATUS may be lost.** The firmware emits the extended
  STATUS frame once at boot. If the Pi-side bridge subscribes after
  the frame has already gone out, the chip-identity dump is lost
  until the next ESP32 reset. Frame counts and IMU samples still
  arrive; only the boot-time chip identity is missing.
* **Diagnostic STATUS frames after IMU recovery.** When `imu::read()`
  fails the firmware calls `imu::begin()` and emits a short STATUS
  frame with the new flags. There is no rate-limit on this STATUS
  frame, so a wedged I²C bus would generate a STATUS frame every
  10 ms (at the IMU deadline). This is benign because (a) STATUS
  frames are small (7 bytes on the wire) and (b) the Pi-side bridge
  caches the most recent STATUS, so the only consequence is a brief
  burst of frame traffic.

## Chapter 4: Pi-Side Hardware Abstraction (`recon_hardware`)

### 4.1 Package structure: mixed C++17 + Python 3.12 in one ROS2 package

`recon_hardware` is unusual among the project's packages in that it
mixes a C++17 executable (`sim_sensor_node`) with two Python modules
(`esp32_uart_bridge.py`, `imu_yaw_integrator.py`) plus a shared parser
(`framing.py`). The rationale (documented in `recon_hardware/__init__.py`
docstring and in the package's `CMakeLists.txt`) is that **both
artefacts are hardware-adjacent** and live conceptually in the same
package even though they have different build systems:

* The C++ side is built by `ament_cmake` and produces a binary
  `sim_sensor_node` installed under `lib/recon_hardware/`.
* The Python side is installed by `ament_python_install_package`,
  which copies the `recon_hardware/` directory tree into the
  workspace `install/` overlay.

This dual nature is made explicit in `CMakeLists.txt`:

```cmake
find_package(ament_cmake_python REQUIRED)
ament_python_install_package(${PROJECT_NAME})

add_executable(sim_sensor_node src/sim_sensor_node.cpp)
ament_target_dependencies(sim_sensor_node rclcpp sensor_msgs nav_msgs)
install(TARGETS sim_sensor_node DESTINATION lib/${PROJECT_NAME})
```

Per `AGENT_RULES.md` §3, C++17 is mandated for hardware paths and
Python 3.12 for non-real-time paths. `sim_sensor_node` is a synthetic
LIDAR data source (used for bench-testing the SLAM pipeline without
real hardware) and is therefore in C++; the bridge and yaw integrator
are I/O-bound and are in Python because pyserial and rclpy ergonomics
are dramatically better there.

### 4.2 `framing.py` — Python mirror of the C++ framing layer

`recon_hardware/framing.py` (268 lines) is the canonical Pi-side
implementation of the binary frame format. It is a direct mirror of
`firmware/esp32/src/framing.cpp` and is kept in sync by a binding rule
in `AGENT_RULES.md` §10 ("Frame format is canonical — Changing the
wire format breaks the Pi-side bridge; coordinate the two sides in one
commit").

Key module-level constants:

```python
SYNC0 = 0xA5
SYNC1 = 0x5A
MAX_PAYLOAD = 64   # matches firmware/esp32/src/framing.h
```

The module exports five enums and one dataclass family:

* `FrameType` — `IntEnum` with values `IMU=0x01, BUTTON=0x02,
  HEARTBEAT=0x03, STATUS=0x04, LIDAR_FRAME=0x05, LIDAR_EN=0x06,
  LIDAR_ACK=0x07`.
* `ButtonId` — `SHUTDOWN=0, STARTSTOP=1, SAVE=2`.
* `ButtonState` — `RELEASED=0, PRESSED=1, LONGPRESS=2`.
* `STATUS_BOOT`, `STATUS_IMU_OK`, `STATUS_IMU_DATA` — flag bit
  constants matching the firmware's `config.h`.
* `ImuSample`, `ButtonEvent`, `StatusFrame` — `@dataclass` containers
  for decoded payloads. `StatusFrame` has optional fields for the
  extended 8-byte boot variant.

#### CRC-8 implementation

The Python implementation of Dallas/Maxim CRC-8 is a direct port:

```python
def crc8(data: bytes) -> int:
    crc = 0
    for byte in data:
        crc ^= byte
        for _ in range(8):
            crc = ((crc << 1) ^ 0x07) & 0xFF if (crc & 0x80) else ((crc << 1) & 0xFF)
    return crc
```

Three known test vectors (`tests/test_esp32_uart_bridge.py::test_crc8_known_vectors`)
exercise it: `crc8(b"") == 0`, `crc8(b"\x01") == 0x07`,
`crc8(b"hello") == 0x92`. The values match the Linux kernel's
`crc8` helper with `polynomial = 0x07`, init `0x00`.

#### `FrameParser` state machine

The Python `FrameParser` (`framing.py:176-267`) implements the same
six-state machine as the C++ side. The public API is byte-oriented:

* `feed(b: int)` — push one byte; returns `None` mid-frame or a
  result tuple when a frame completes.
* `feed_bytes(chunk: bytes)` — generator that yields each completed
  frame from a multi-byte buffer.

Result tuples come in four shapes:

1. `(FrameType.X, decoded_payload)` for a successful frame.
2. `("CRC_FAIL", (ftype, flen, expected_crc, got_crc))` when CRC
   validation fails.
3. `("BAD_LEN", (ftype, len, payload))` when a frame's LEN field
   does not match the expected length for its type.
4. `("UNKNOWN", (ftype, payload))` for an unrecognised TYPE byte.

A `_PAYLOAD_LENGTHS` dict pins valid payload lengths per known
opcode: `IMU={24}`, `BUTTON={2}`, `HEARTBEAT={4}`, `STATUS={2, 8}`,
`LIDAR_ACK={1}`. `LIDAR_FRAME` is intentionally absent from the dict
because its payload is arbitrary (any chunk from the LD14P byte
stream, 1..64 bytes); the parser's `_dispatch` accepts any size.

#### Encode helpers

Two Pi → ESP encoders are exported:

* `encode_frame(ftype, payload=b"")` — generic builder. Raises
  `ValueError` if `payload` exceeds `MAX_PAYLOAD`.
* `encode_lidar_en(enable: bool)` — convenience wrapper that returns
  the wire bytes for a `LIDAR_EN` frame with a single byte payload
  of `0x01` (enable) or `0x00` (disable). The `esp32_uart_bridge`
  service handler uses this exclusively when writing to the serial
  port.

### 4.3 `esp32_uart_bridge.py` — complete analysis

The bridge is the largest single Python file in the workspace at
494 lines. Its responsibilities are:

1. Open `/dev/ttyUSB0` at 460 800 baud, with retry-on-failure.
2. Parse incoming frames using `FrameParser` and demux them to four
   classes of output: ROS topics, JSON diagnostics, the LIDAR pty,
   and internal counters.
3. Expose a `/lidar_enable` service (`std_srvs/SetBool`) that
   propagates motor-state commands from the Pi-side stack down to
   the firmware over the same serial link.
4. Refresh `LIDAR_EN=1` every 1 second while the motor is enabled,
   so the firmware's 3-second watchdog never trips.
5. Hold a pty whose slave path is symlinked to `/tmp/lidar_pty`,
   into which raw LD14P bytes are forwarded for consumption by the
   `ldlidar_stl_ros2` driver.
6. Publish a JSON `/esp32/diagnostics` payload at 1 Hz summarising
   port state, frame counts, motor state, and chip identity.

The constructor (`Esp32UartBridge.__init__`) declares six ROS
parameters with defaults that match `config/esp32_bridge.yaml`:

| Parameter         | Default            | Effect                                                     |
| ----------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `port`            | `/dev/ttyUSB0`     | Serial device path                                         |
| `baud`            | `460800`           | UART baud                                                  |
| `frame_id`        | `imu_link`         | `sensor_msgs/Imu` header frame                             |
| `diag_period_s`   | `1.0`              | Diagnostics publish period                                 |
| `quiet_imu_warn`  | `false`            | Suppress per-frame CRC-fail logs                           |
| `lidar_refresh_s` | `1.0`              | Period of LIDAR_EN=1 refresh while motor is on             |
| `lidar_pty_link`  | `/tmp/lidar_pty`   | Symlink target for the pty slave                           |

#### Serial-port discovery and opening

The reader thread (`_reader_loop`) imports `pyserial` lazily and
attempts to open the port in a backoff retry loop: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s,
capped at 10 s. The 0.2 s timeout on `serial.Serial(...)` ensures the
`ser.read(128)` call below cannot block indefinitely. Once the port
opens, the reader publishes `self._port_open = True`, stashes the
serial handle in `self._serial` (so the writer side of the
`/lidar_enable` service can use it), and enters the inner read loop.

#### Read loop threading model

The read loop runs in a **real Python OS thread** (`threading.Thread`
with `daemon=True`). It is intentionally separate from the rclpy
executor because pyserial's blocking `read()` would otherwise stall
the executor's callback dispatch. Frames parsed by `FrameParser` are
dispatched to `_handle_frame`, which runs on the same OS thread.
`_handle_frame` calls `rclpy.publisher.publish` — which is documented
as thread-safe in rclpy — directly. No locks are held across the
publish.

The reader has a two-tier exception scope. The inner `try` catches
`serial.SerialException` or `OSError` (port errors) and propagates
them to the outer connect-and-retry loop. A second nested `try` wraps
the frame-handler call so that a bug in dispatch (e.g. an unexpected
payload format) does not silently kill the thread; the exception is
logged with `throttle_duration_sec=1.0` and the next frame is read.
The reader thread also catches *any* unexpected exception, logs it
loudly with `exc_info=True`, and reopens the port.

#### Frame demuxing

The dispatch in `_handle_frame` is a straight-line `if/elif` chain by
frame type. Counters in `self._counts` are bumped for every frame
class. Significant branches:

* **IMU.** `_publish_imu(sample)` constructs a `sensor_msgs/Imu`
  message with the stamp from the bridge node's clock (not the
  ESP32's wall clock — the ESP32 has no real-time clock; the bridge
  applies the Pi-side time which is the only timing source SLAM and
  the EKF can trust). `linear_acceleration` and `angular_velocity`
  are filled from the parsed `ImuSample`; the orientation field and
  the covariance matrices are left at their default zero values (the
  yaw integrator and EKF will populate orientation downstream).
* **BUTTON.** `_publish_button(evt)` records the event in a
  ring-buffer (`self._last_button_events`, last 8 events for the
  diagnostics card) and publishes a `std_msgs/Empty` on one of four
  topics depending on the button and state:
  * `(SAVE, PRESSED)` → `/buttons/save`
  * `(STARTSTOP, PRESSED)` → `/buttons/startstop`
  * `(SHUTDOWN, PRESSED)` → `/buttons/shutdown_request`
  * `(SHUTDOWN, LONGPRESS)` → `/buttons/shutdown_longpress`
  RELEASED is recorded for diagnostics but does not generate a topic
  publication.
* **HEARTBEAT.** Stores `uptime_ms` in `self._last_heartbeat_ms`
  for the diagnostics payload.
* **STATUS.** Stores the parsed `StatusFrame` in
  `self._last_status` and logs the chip identity at `INFO` level.
* **LIDAR_FRAME.** Bumps `lidar_frame` and `lidar_bytes` counters
  and forwards the bytes to the pty via `_write_lidar_bytes`.
* **LIDAR_ACK.** Updates `self._lidar_acked` and emits an `INFO`-
  level log on state change.
* **CRC_FAIL / BAD_LEN.** Bumps the matching counter and logs at
  DEBUG level (unless `quiet_imu_warn` is set, in which case CRC
  failures are silent — useful when running on a noisy bench
  cable).

#### PTY master/slave construction

The LIDAR data path uses a Unix pseudo-tty pair. `pty.openpty()`
returns a master file descriptor and a slave fd. The bridge:

1. Calls `os.ttyname(slave_fd)` to discover the slave's `/dev/pts/N`
   path.
2. Calls `tty.setraw(master_fd, termios.TCSANOW)` to put the master
   in raw mode (no canonical line-buffering, no echo).
3. Sets the master fd non-blocking with `fcntl.F_SETFL | O_NONBLOCK`
   so writes that race ahead of the reader return `EAGAIN` rather
   than blocking the reader thread.
4. Closes the slave fd immediately — the kernel keeps the slave
   path openable as long as we hold the master.
5. Unlinks any stale `/tmp/lidar_pty` and creates a fresh symlink to
   the slave path.

Writes to the master (`_write_lidar_bytes`) use `os.write(fd, data)`.
On `BlockingIOError` (`EAGAIN`) the chunk is dropped and
`self._pty_overflow_count` is incremented. This is a deliberate trade:
during the startup race window before the `ldlidar_stl_ros2` driver
opens the slave, several KB of `LIDAR_FRAME` data can pile up at the
master. Rather than buffer indefinitely (which would leak memory) or
block (which would stall the reader thread), the bridge drops bytes
the LD14P would have re-emitted on the next rotation anyway. The
documented impact is "initial pty overflows during startup race"
(`REMAINING_ISSUES.md` L5, `STATUS.md` §7 #4) — once the driver opens
the slave, the kernel pty buffer keeps both sides in lockstep and the
overflow counter stops growing.

#### `/lidar_enable` service handler

The service is `std_srvs/SetBool` with `request.data: bool`. On call:

1. Update `self._lidar_desired = req.data`.
2. Synchronously write a `LIDAR_EN` frame on the open serial port via
   `_send_lidar_en`. Returns `False` if the port is not open right now
   (the caller decides whether to retry).
3. Set `resp.success = ok` and `resp.message` to a status string.

The pairing with the periodic refresh timer (`_refresh_lidar`) is
deliberate: the *service call* sends a single `LIDAR_EN` frame
immediately, and the *timer* re-asserts `LIDAR_EN=1` once a second
thereafter while the motor is on. If the desired state is False, the
timer does nothing — the firmware's watchdog will drop the motor
within 3 s anyway.

#### Diagnostics publisher

`_emit_diagnostics` is called by a 1 Hz wall-clock timer. It locks
`self._lock`, snapshots the counters and the last-status, builds a
dict containing:

* `port`, `baud`, `port_open` — link health.
* `frame_counts` — running totals per opcode plus CRC/length errors.
* `seconds_since_last_frame` — wall-clock seconds since any frame
  arrived; used by the UI as a "link healthy?" indicator.
* `esp32_uptime_ms` — last received heartbeat value.
* `recent_buttons` — list of the last 8 button events.
* `lidar` — sub-dict with `desired_on`, `acked_on`, `frames`,
  `bytes`, `pty_slave`, `pty_link`, `pty_overflows`.
* `status` — parsed STATUS payload with derived `afs_sel` /
  `fs_sel` values (decoded from the configuration bytes).

The dict is serialised to JSON with compact separators
(`(",", ":")`) and published on `/esp32/diagnostics`.

#### Clean shutdown

`destroy_node()` is overridden to (a) request the LIDAR motor off
(best-effort), (b) unlink the `/tmp/lidar_pty` symlink so the next
run starts fresh, (c) close the master fd, (d) signal `self._stop`
to the reader thread, and (e) `join` the reader with a 1.5 s
timeout.

### 4.4 `imu_yaw_integrator.py` — gyro-Z → quaternion republisher

The MPU-6050 publishes only raw accelerometer and gyroscope data; it
has no magnetometer (the chip is 6-axis, not 9-axis), so there is no
absolute heading reference. The `imu_yaw_integrator` node bridges the
gap between `/imu/data_raw` (which lacks an orientation quaternion)
and `/imu/data` (which slam_toolbox subscribes to and expects to have
the orientation field populated).

#### Why gyro integration instead of full AHRS?

A full Attitude-and-Heading Reference System (AHRS) such as
Madgwick or Mahony fuses accelerometer-based roll/pitch with
gyro-integrated yaw to give a drift-corrected three-axis orientation.
The Recon-Platform-R2 project chose **gyro-only yaw integration** for
three reasons:

1. **No magnetometer to fight drift.** Without magnetic data, yaw is
   gyro-only regardless of which AHRS variant is used.
2. **Accelerometer bias is large.** The chip's factory ZA_OFFSET
   biases the accelerometer Z reading by ~5.5 m/s²; feeding this into
   a Madgwick filter would estimate a tilted gravity vector and bias
   the roll/pitch estimate.
3. **2-D scanning doesn't need roll/pitch.** The LIDAR scans a
   horizontal plane; a few degrees of tilt translates to a sub-cm
   range error and is well within the SLAM matcher's tolerance.

The integrator therefore outputs a quaternion in which roll and pitch
are exactly zero and yaw is the integrated gyro Z. Drift accumulates
at the order of a few degrees per minute (`STATUS.md` §6 quotes
"theta drifting at ~0.7 °/s with the chip's uncalibrated gyro bias")
but slam_toolbox's scan matcher continuously corrects yaw against the
LIDAR data, and a successful scan match erases the drift accumulated
since the previous match.

#### Integration step

The pure-function `integrate_yaw(prev_yaw, gyro_z, dt)` is the heart
of the node:

```python
def integrate_yaw(prev_yaw: float, gyro_z: float, dt: float) -> float:
    if dt <= 0.0 or dt > 1.0:
        return prev_yaw
    new_yaw = prev_yaw + float(gyro_z) * float(dt)
    new_yaw = math.fmod(new_yaw + math.pi, 2.0 * math.pi)
    if new_yaw <= 0.0:
        new_yaw += 2.0 * math.pi
    return new_yaw - math.pi
```

* `dt ≤ 0 or > 1` returns the previous yaw unchanged. The lower bound
  catches degenerate "two messages with the same stamp" cases; the
  upper bound catches sensor dropouts where the previous timestamp is
  more than a second old.
* `math.fmod` wraps the angle to `(-π, π]`. The two-step adjustment
  (add π, modulo 2π, subtract π) is the standard way to wrap into
  the principal value range using `fmod`'s implementation-defined
  behaviour on negative operands.

#### Quaternion construction

```python
def yaw_to_quaternion_xyzw(yaw: float) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    half = 0.5 * yaw
    return (0.0, 0.0, math.sin(half), math.cos(half))
```

This is the standard 2-D yaw rotation about the Z axis. The output is
unit-length by construction (`sin² + cos² = 1`). The pytest case
`test_quaternion_unit_norm` verifies that the norm-squared is exactly
1.0 (within `1e-9`) for several yaw values.

#### Subscription QoS

The input `/imu/data_raw` is published with `BEST_EFFORT` QoS by the
bridge (matching the 100 Hz IMU stream, where retransmission of lost
samples is more expensive than the next sample). The integrator
subscribes with `BEST_EFFORT` to match (otherwise the subscription
silently fails to connect; ROS2 QoS-incompatibility is a documented
gotcha). It re-publishes on `/imu/data` with the default `RELIABLE`
QoS because slam_toolbox subscribes there with reliable QoS.

#### Orientation covariance

The output IMU message sets the diagonal of the orientation covariance
matrix to:

* `[0] = 0.05 rad²` (roll, unknown)
* `[4] = 0.05 rad²` (pitch, unknown)
* `[8] = 0.10 rad²` (yaw, gyro drift)

The non-zero values tell downstream EKFs "this orientation is an
estimate, not a measurement — use it as a prior but be willing to
correct". A diagonal of all zeros would be interpreted by
`robot_localization` as "no information about orientation", whereas
the specific values express the relative confidences.

### 4.5 `sim_sensor_node.cpp` — simulated LIDAR for bench testing

`recon_hardware/src/sim_sensor_node.cpp` is a C++17 ROS2 node that
generates a synthetic 360-beam `LaserScan` and publishes it on
`/scan` at 10 Hz. It is used in workflows where the real LD14P is not
present (e.g. when bench-testing slam_toolbox or the web UI's
rendering pipeline). It is **not** used in any of the `setup.sh`
modes that the user normally runs; it is invoked manually for
diagnostic work.

The node generates a randomised walled room with optional internal
partitions and rectangular obstacles, then raycasts a LaserScan from
a configurable fixed spawn pose. It deliberately does **not** track
motion: there is no pose subscription, no integration of velocity, no
synthetic motion model. The intent is to exercise slam_toolbox
startup, the web UI map renderer, and the headless save pipeline
under fully deterministic conditions.

Configuration is via ROS parameters loaded from
`config/simulation.yaml`. The room generation phase consists of three
sub-steps:

1. **Outer walls.** A 2-cell-thick perimeter is painted as occupied
   (`grid_[y*w + x] = 100`).
2. **Internal partitions.** A random count between
   `min_partitions=1` and `max_partitions=3` is chosen. Each
   partition is either horizontal or vertical (random), and a
   doorway gap of `doorway_width_m / resolution` cells is punched
   through it at a random along-axis position.
3. **Obstacles.** A random count between `min_obstacles=4` and
   `max_obstacles=8` rectangular obstacles is placed, each with
   random width and height in `[obstacle_min_size_m,
   obstacle_max_size_m]`. Obstacles within 8 cells of the spawn
   pose are rejected (to keep the spawn area clear).
4. **Reachability cleanup.** A BFS flood fill from the spawn cell
   identifies the reachable free area. If fewer than 70 % of free
   cells are reachable, any wall cells inside the interior that are
   not reachable from spawn are reset to free, on the assumption
   that they trapped the spawn pose inside a small pocket.

The raycast loop (`raycast(ox, oy, angle, max_range)`) is a fixed-
step grid walker. The step size is `resolution * 0.5` (so half a
cell). The number of steps is `max_range / step`. At each step the
position is advanced by `(cos(angle), sin(angle)) * step`, the grid
cell is looked up, and if the cell is occupied (`grid_[...] > 50`)
the function returns the Euclidean distance from origin to the hit
point. If no occupied cell is reached within `max_range`, the
function returns `max_range`.

The synthetic LaserScan has 360 beams (one per degree),
`angle_min = -π`, `angle_max = +π`, additive Gaussian noise with
`stddev = 0.005 m`, and a fixed scan rate of 10 Hz. The ground-truth
OccupancyGrid is also published at 0.5 Hz on `/sim/ground_truth`
for debug visualisation.

### 4.6 robot_localization EKF node

`robot_localization` is the third-party ROS2 package that supplies
the EKF used by Recon-Platform-R2 to convert IMU yaw into an `/odom`
topic and an `odom→base_link` TF. The node executable is
`ros2 run robot_localization ekf_node`, configured by
`config/ekf.yaml` (parsed in detail in §6.2 and Appendix D).

The EKF is invoked from `setup.sh launch_ekf()`:

```bash
ros2 run robot_localization ekf_node \
    --ros-args --params-file ${SCRIPT_DIR}/config/ekf.yaml \
    -r /odometry/filtered:=/odom
```

The remap `/odometry/filtered:=/odom` is necessary because the EKF
defaults its output topic to `/odometry/filtered`; slam_toolbox and
the web UI both look for `/odom` by convention, so the remap aligns
the topic name.

The configuration declares a single input source: `imu0: /imu/data`.
The `imu0_config` is a 15-element boolean vector that selects which
of `[x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw, vx, vy, vz, vroll, vpitch, vyaw, ax,
ay, az]` are fused. Only **yaw** (index 5) and **vyaw** (index 11)
are set to True; all other slots — including all linear acceleration
fields — are False.

The reasoning is given in `ekf.yaml`:

> * The MPU-6050 has no magnetometer — Madgwick roll/pitch are
>   accel-corrected but yaw is gyro-only anyway.
> * The chip's factory ZA_OFFSET makes linear_acceleration unreliable
>   (gravity reads ~15 m/s² flat instead of 9.81). Fusing accel here
>   would integrate that bias into runaway position drift.
> * For 2-D handheld scanning, translation comes from slam_toolbox's
>   scan matching, not IMU dead-reckoning. EKF only needs to supply
>   the yaw prior + odom frame.

The result is an EKF that tracks only orientation, not translation.
`/odom` exposes a pose whose `x, y` components stay at the origin and
whose `theta` integrates from gyro Z. slam_toolbox's `map → odom` TF
provides the translation correction at scan rate, and the web UI
composes `map → odom ∘ odom → base_link` to get the device pose for
display.

The EKF runs at 30 Hz (`frequency: 30.0`), publishes the
`odom → base_link` TF (`publish_tf: true`), operates in 2-D mode
(`two_d_mode: true`), and starts at yaw = 0 (`imu0_relative: true`).

#### TF tree

The full TF tree during `setup.sh full` is:

```
            (slam_toolbox publishes)
            map ──► odom
                     │ (ekf_node from /imu/data)
                     ▼
                  base_link
                     │ (static, from ldlidar launch)
                     ▼
                 laser_frame
```

In addition, `setup.sh launch_imu_link_tf` publishes a static
identity `base_link → imu_link` so that the `frame_id` on the
`sensor_msgs/Imu` message resolves correctly. The enclosure stage
(H6) will replace the identity with a real mechanical offset between
the device's base reference and the IMU PCB.
