## Chapter 9: System Integration and Deployment

### 9.1 `setup.sh` — complete analysis

`setup.sh` is the canonical entry point for starting the stack
(`AGENT_RULES.md` §9). It is a 663-line Bash script that supports
six modes:

| Mode          | What it brings up                                                                                |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `kill`        | Tears down tmux session + stale recon processes, then exits.                                     |
| `demo`        | Web UI only, mock data — no ROS2, no DB.                                                          |
| `web`         | Web UI + DB node, ROS2 running, no hardware.                                                      |
| `imu-test`    | ESP32 bridge + yaw integrator + EKF + static `base_link→imu_link` TF + DB + Web UI.               |
| `sensor-test` | LIDAR + slam_toolbox + (ESP32 bridge+EKF, optional) + DB + Web UI. Pass `--no-esp32` for LIDAR-only. |
| `full`        | **The canonical scanning mode.** LIDAR + ESP32 + yaw integrator + IMU TF + EKF + slam_toolbox + DB + Web UI. |

**[DISCREPANCY: copilot-instructions.md scripts table]**: the table
lists only four modes (`kill`, `demo`, `web`, `sensor-test`). The
current `setup.sh` has six modes (the table above). The
`copilot-instructions.md` was written before H3 (imu-test) and
H4-prep (full) were added.

#### tmux session structure

Each launched node runs in a dedicated tmux window inside a single
tmux session named `recon`. The session is created lazily by
`start_in_tmux`:

```bash
start_in_tmux() {
    local window_name="$1"
    shift
    local cmd="$*"
    if ! tmux has-session -t "$TMUX_SESSION" 2>/dev/null; then
        tmux new-session -d -s "$TMUX_SESSION" -n "$window_name"
    else
        tmux new-window -t "$TMUX_SESSION" -n "$window_name"
    fi
    tmux send-keys -t "$TMUX_SESSION:$window_name" "$cmd" C-m
}
```

Window names by mode (the user attaches to the session with
`tmux attach -t recon`):

| Mode `full` windows | Purpose                              |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `esp32`             | `esp32_uart_bridge` (IMU + LIDAR relay) |
| `imu_yaw`           | `imu_yaw_integrator`                 |
| `imu_tf`            | static `base_link → imu_link` TF     |
| `ekf`               | `robot_localization ekf_node`        |
| `lidar`             | `ldlidar_stl_ros2_node`              |
| `slam_tb`           | `slam_toolbox` online async          |
| `db_node`           | `db_node`                            |
| `webui`             | Flask + SocketIO server              |

#### Per-pane venv activation and the `ModuleNotFoundError` issue

Every command is built up from two helper functions:

```bash
source_ros2_cmd() {
    echo "deactivate 2>/dev/null; unset VIRTUAL_ENV; source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && source ${SCRIPT_DIR}/install/setup.bash 2>/dev/null; "
}

venv_ros2_cmd() {
    local prefix=""
    if [[ -f "${SCRIPT_DIR}/.venv/bin/activate" ]]; then
        prefix="source ${SCRIPT_DIR}/.venv/bin/activate && "
    fi
    echo "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && source ${SCRIPT_DIR}/install/setup.bash 2>/dev/null && ${prefix}"
}
```

The `venv_ros2_cmd` form is used for Python ROS2 nodes that need
both ROS2 *and* the project venv (sqlalchemy, eventlet, pyserial,
etc.). The `source_ros2_cmd` form is used for C++ ROS2 launches
that do **not** need the venv (and where activating it might cause
problems if the venv's pyserial or numpy versions disagree with
the system Python that the C++ binary indirectly invokes).

The reason this matters is documented in `AGENT_RULES.md` §9:

> Bare `ros2 launch recon_bringup full_system.launch.py` / `ros2
> run recon_webui recon_webui` will spawn subprocesses that do NOT
> inherit the venv → `ModuleNotFoundError: sqlalchemy/eventlet`.
> Confirmed empirically; don't relearn.

`setup.sh` is the only path that correctly activates the venv per
tmux window.

#### Pre-flight stty on `/dev/ttyUSB0`

The `launch_esp32_bridge` function includes a pre-flight `stty`
command that forces the USB-Serial device into raw 460800 8N1
before the bridge opens it:

```bash
local pre_stty="if [[ -e /dev/ttyUSB0 ]]; then stty -F /dev/ttyUSB0 460800 raw -echo cs8 -parenb -cstopb 2>/dev/null || true; fi"
start_in_tmux "esp32" "${pre_stty} && $(venv_ros2_cmd)python3 -m recon_hardware.esp32_uart_bridge ..."
```

This was added in the auto-start commit (2026-05-26) after a
documented incident where systemd-launched boots opened the port
successfully but received zero bytes. The kernel had left stale
TTY mode flags (XON/XOFF flow control, cooked mode, echo) from a
previous boot, and pyserial's defaults did not override them
aggressively enough at first open. The explicit `stty` reset
forces the device into a known state.

#### Bind-port preflight

Before launching any node, `setup.sh` checks whether the system
`python3` has the `cap_net_bind_service` capability. If it does
not (which happens after every `apt upgrade` of `python3.12`), the
script exports `WEBUI_PORT=8080` with a warning. The web UI then
binds to 8080 instead of 80 and the user can still access it
(though they have to type the port in the URL).

#### Mode-specific launch sequences

Each mode's launch sequence is a sequence of `launch_*` calls with
`sleep` interludes. The intervals are tuned to allow node
discovery (DDS) to settle before the next node tries to connect.

The `full` mode launch order:

```bash
ensure_db                      # docker compose up -d; wait for pg_isready
launch_esp32_bridge            # ESP32 bridge — opens /dev/ttyUSB0
sleep 1
launch_imu_yaw_integrator      # subscribes to /imu/data_raw
sleep 1
launch_imu_link_tf             # static base_link → imu_link
sleep 1
launch_ekf                     # ekf_node — subscribes to /imu/data
sleep 1
launch_lidar_node              # ldlidar_stl_ros2 — opens /tmp/lidar_pty
sleep 2                        # extra time for pty subscription
launch_slam_toolbox            # slam_toolbox — subscribes to /scan
sleep 2
launch_db_node                 # db_node — subscribes to /map etc.
sleep 1
launch_webui_ros               # Flask + SocketIO + rclpy bridge
```

The order matters: the bridge must be up before the yaw integrator
subscribes to its output; the integrator must be up before
slam_toolbox subscribes to `/imu/data`; the EKF must be up before
slam_toolbox tries to look up `odom → base_link`. The 1- and 2-
second delays absorb DDS discovery latency.

### 9.2 `environment.sh` — idempotent provisioning

`environment.sh` is a 902-line Bash script that bootstraps a fresh
Pi 5 from a stock Ubuntu Server 24.04 install. It has two modes:
default install + verify, and `--check` (verify-only).

The script is structured as a sequence of numbered sections:

* **Section 0: apt lock wait.** Polls for `unattended-upgrades` or
  any other apt process to release the dpkg lock, with a 5-minute
  timeout.
* **Section 1: System packages.** Installs git, curl, wget, tmux,
  build-essential, cmake, python3-{pip,venv,dev}, ca-certificates,
  unzip, locales. Generates `en_US.UTF-8` locale.
* **Section 2: LIDAR UART setup.** Configures the Pi's PL011 UART
  for the LIDAR (see §2.2). This is preserved post-pivot even
  though the LIDAR no longer uses the Pi UART directly, so that
  `sensor-test --no-esp32` still works as a fallback.
* **Section 3: ROS2 Jazzy.** Adds the ROS2 apt repo, installs
  `ros-jazzy-ros-base`.
* **Section 4: ROS2 packages.** Installs `slam-toolbox`,
  `robot-localization`, the message packages (`sensor-msgs`,
  `geometry-msgs`, `nav-msgs`, `std-msgs`, `std-srvs`),
  `tf2-ros`, `tf2-msgs`, `ament-cmake-gtest`, `rclcpp`, `rclpy`,
  `colcon-common-extensions`, `python3-serial`, `libgtest-dev`.
  Notably absent: `imu-filter-madgwick` (we use our own yaw
  integrator instead).
* **Section 5: Python venv.** Creates `roomba_ws/.venv` with
  `--system-site-packages` (so the venv can see system rclpy
  while still hosting Python deps from `requirements.txt`).
  Installs `requirements.txt`: flask, flask-socketio,
  flask-sqlalchemy, sqlalchemy, psycopg2-binary, alembic, numpy,
  opencv-python-headless, pytest, pyyaml, eventlet.
  **[DISCREPANCY: requirements.txt vs runtime use]**: the
  requirements include `opencv-python-headless>=4.9` but no code
  in the post-pivot stack imports OpenCV. `postprocess.py` is
  pure NumPy. The dependency is vestigial and can be removed.
* **Section 6: WiFi AP + networking.** Already covered in §8.7.
  Includes the `cap_net_bind_service` setcap and the ldconfig
  registration.
* **Section 7: Docker + PostgreSQL.** Installs Docker (if not
  present), starts the `roomba_postgres` container.
* **Section 8: Workspace build.** Runs `colcon build
  --symlink-install`. Warnings are logged but do not fail the
  script.
* **Section 9: Shell environment.** Appends ROS2 sourcing, venv
  activation, and `RECON_DB_URL` export to `~/.bashrc`.
* **Section 9.5: Auto-start systemd unit.** Installs
  `roomba_ws/systemd/recon-stack.service` to
  `/etc/systemd/system/`, runs `daemon-reload`, enables the unit.
  Re-copies on every run if the template differs.
* **Section 10 (always runs): Verification.** ~100 checks across
  11 categories (Core Software, ROS2 Packages, Python venv,
  Docker + PostgreSQL, LIDAR UART, WiFi AP + Networking,
  Auto-start, Workspace & Build, Config Files, Web UI Assets,
  Shell Environment, Test Skeletons).

The verification helpers `check`, `check_warn`, and `check_sudo`
classify each test as PASS / FAIL / WARN. `check_sudo` is the
helper added in commit `dc4c501` to fix `REMAINING_ISSUES.md` M5:
if `sudo -n true` fails (no cached sudo), the check emits WARN
rather than FAIL, with a hint to run `sudo -v` first.

### 9.3 `recon-stack.service` — systemd auto-start

`roomba_ws/systemd/recon-stack.service` runs `setup.sh full` at
boot. The unit declares:

* `After=network-online.target docker.service recon-ap.service` —
  waits for network, Docker daemon, and the WiFi AP before
  starting.
* `Wants=network-online.target docker.service` — soft dependency
  (will start regardless if these are missing, but normally waits
  for them).
* `Type=simple`, `User=gabi`, `Group=gabi`,
  `WorkingDirectory=/home/gabi/Recon-Platform-R2/roomba_ws`.
* `ExecStartPre=/bin/bash -c 'for i in $(seq 1 30); do [ -e
  /dev/ttyUSB0 ] && exit 0; sleep 1; done; ...'` — waits up to 30
  seconds for the ESP32 USB-Serial bridge to enumerate, but does
  not fail the unit if it doesn't appear (setup.sh's pre-flight
  checks emit clearer messages).
* `ExecStart=/bin/bash setup.sh full` — the canonical entry point.
* `KillMode=mixed`, `TimeoutStopSec=20` — SIGTERM to the main
  process triggers `setup.sh`'s trap (tmux teardown +
  kill_stale_processes); cgroup-wide SIGKILL is the safety net
  if the graceful teardown stalls.
* `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=15`,
  `StartLimitBurst=5`, `StartLimitIntervalSec=300` — five
  restart attempts in a five-minute window before giving up.
* `Environment=HOME=/home/gabi USER=gabi LANG=en_US.UTF-8` —
  minimal environment.
* `WantedBy=multi-user.target` — enabled at boot.

### 9.4 `rebuild.sh` — colcon convenience wrapper

`rebuild.sh` is a 96-line helper that wraps `colcon build`. It
supports shorthand package names (`web` → `recon_webui`, etc.) and
a `clean` mode that wipes `build/`, `install/`, and `log/` first.

A quirk: the `PKG_ALIASES` map still references pre-pivot package
names (`nav=roomba_navigation`, `hw=roomba_hardware`,
`web=roomba_webui`, `ctrl=roomba_control`, `db=roomba_db`,
`bringup=roomba_bringup`). These are stale; the actual package
directories are `recon_*`. The aliases work only for direct package
names (`./rebuild.sh recon_webui`), not the shorthand
(`./rebuild.sh web`), because the alias resolves to
`roomba_webui`, which doesn't exist.

**[DISCREPANCY: `rebuild.sh` PKG_ALIASES vs actual package names]**.

### 9.5 Docker integration

The PostgreSQL container is the only Docker workload. It is started
by `setup.sh ensure_db` via `docker compose up -d` in the
`docker/` directory. The container's port 5432 is bound to
`127.0.0.1:5432` so the recon nodes (running on the Pi host) can
connect via `localhost:5432` and the database is not exposed on
the AP or LAN.

The lifecycle of the container is independent of `recon-stack.service`:
the container is started by `setup.sh` and stays running across
`recon-stack.service` restarts (`restart: unless-stopped`). A clean
shutdown of the Pi (`shutdown -h now`) does call Docker's stop
sequence, which gracefully stops the container.

### 9.6 `requirements.txt`

The Python dependency manifest is short:

```
flask>=3.0
flask-socketio>=5.3
flask-sqlalchemy>=3.1
sqlalchemy>=2.0
psycopg2-binary>=2.9
alembic>=1.13
numpy>=1.26
opencv-python-headless>=4.9
pytest>=8.0
pyyaml>=6.0
eventlet>=0.35
```

Reasons per package:

* **flask, flask-socketio.** The web framework and SocketIO server.
* **flask-sqlalchemy.** Imported but not actually used post-pivot;
  the project uses raw SQLAlchemy via `recon_db.models`. Vestigial.
* **sqlalchemy.** The ORM.
* **psycopg2-binary.** PostgreSQL driver. The `-binary` suffix
  ships pre-compiled wheels and avoids needing libpq-dev at build
  time.
* **alembic.** Schema migration framework (scaffolded but not
  driving).
* **numpy.** Required for `recon_db.postprocess` and for parsing
  IMU floats in the bridge.
* **opencv-python-headless.** Listed but unused post-pivot
  (see `[DISCREPANCY]` above).
* **pytest.** Test runner.
* **pyyaml.** Used by `recon_webui.app.load_webui_config()` to
  read `config/webui.yaml`.
* **eventlet.** The async runtime that everything in `recon_webui`
  depends on.

`pyserial` is not in `requirements.txt` because it is installed
via apt (`python3-serial`) and the venv has
`--system-site-packages` set, so the apt package is visible to the
venv. This is a deliberate choice documented in
`environment.sh` Section 4 comment.

## Chapter 10: Testing Strategy

### 10.1 Test philosophy

The project's binding rule on testing is `AGENT_RULES.md` §7:
"Every node has at least one test ... Real assertions are mandatory;
a test that always passes is not a test ... Test the contract, not
the implementation". The actual test suite consists of seven files
totalling 1113 lines and 59 test cases:

| File                                  | Cases | Subject                                                     |
| ------------------------------------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tests/test_db_node.py`               | 9     | SQLAlchemy ORM models, CRUD, session-map relationship       |
| `tests/test_recon_webui.py`           | 6     | DataChannel fallback timing, mock data shape                |
| `tests/test_esp32_uart_bridge.py`     | 12    | UART framing parser — CRC, round-trips, resync, error paths |
| `tests/test_imu_yaw_integrator.py`    | 12    | Integration step (clamp, wrap), quaternion form, unit norm |
| `tests/test_postprocess.py`           | 20    | Tier-2 pipeline — median, morphology, components, Hough     |
| `tests/test_draw_node.cpp`            | 4     | OccupancyGrid layout, paint, clear, brush-size clamp        |
| `tests/test_sim_sensor_node.cpp`      | 4     | Raycast hit, max range, room connectivity, obstacle block   |

What is **explicitly not tested**:

* Full rclpy node integration (no rclpy fixtures or
  `rclpy_test_helper`-style harnesses).
* Live serial port behaviour of `esp32_uart_bridge` (only the
  parser is unit-testable without hardware).
* The `clear_map()` / `set_scanning()` round-trips through real
  service clients (`REMAINING_ISSUES.md` M2 fix #3 proposes adding
  a test that simulates calling a helper from an rclpy timer
  callback to verify the assertion).
* The web UI client-side JavaScript (no Selenium / Playwright
  harness).
* End-to-end SLAM accuracy (H4 walking-test deliverable).

### 10.2 `test_esp32_uart_bridge.py` — frame parser coverage

The 12 cases:

1. `test_crc8_known_vectors` — `crc8(b"") == 0`,
   `crc8(b"\x01") == 0x07`, `crc8(b"hello") == 0x92`.
2. `test_crc8_deterministic` — `crc8(a) == crc8(a)` for a 24-byte
   input.
3. `test_imu_roundtrip` — encode an IMU payload with a known
   `az=9.80665` and `gx=0.1`, parse it, assert the values
   round-trip.
4. `test_button_roundtrip` — encode `BUTTON(SAVE, PRESSED)`, parse,
   assert names match.
5. `test_heartbeat_roundtrip` — encode uptime 12 345 ms, parse,
   assert equality.
6. `test_status_short_roundtrip` — 2-byte STATUS variant with
   `flags = BOOT | IMU_OK`.
7. `test_status_diag_roundtrip` — 8-byte extended STATUS variant
   with `who_am_i=0x68`, `accel_cfg=0x08`, `gyro_cfg=0x08`,
   `za_offset_before=1544`, `za_offset_after=0`.
8. `test_resync_after_garbage_prefix` — garbage bytes including a
   stray `0xA5` before a valid frame; the parser must emit
   exactly one heartbeat.
9. `test_consecutive_syncs_still_parse` — `0xA5 0xA5 0x5A ...`
   (the parser's HUNT1 stay-armed branch).
10. `test_bad_crc_emits_crc_fail_and_recovers` — corrupt a frame's
    CRC, then append a good frame; assert `("CRC_FAIL", ...)`
    followed by a successful parse.
11. `test_oversized_len_field_is_dropped` — `LEN=0xFF` is rejected;
    a subsequent good frame parses.
12. `test_chunked_feed` — byte-at-a-time feed produces identical
    output to a single-blob feed.

These cover all four pre-Increment-1 frame types (IMU, BUTTON,
HEARTBEAT, STATUS) and the parser's error paths. The
post-Increment opcodes (LIDAR_FRAME, LIDAR_EN, LIDAR_ACK) are not
covered — this is `REMAINING_ISSUES.md` M1.

### 10.3 `test_imu_yaw_integrator.py` — integration math

The 12 cases verify the pure-function integrator and the
quaternion converter:

1. `test_zero_dt_returns_unchanged` — `integrate_yaw(1.234, 5.0,
   0.0) == 1.234`.
2. `test_negative_dt_returns_unchanged` — same with `dt = -0.001`.
3. `test_huge_dt_returns_unchanged` — `dt = 1.5` (over the 1.0 s
   clamp).
4. `test_normal_integration_step` — `ω_z = 0.1` for `dt = 0.01`
   gives `+0.001 rad`.
5. `test_negative_gyro_decrements_yaw` — `(0.5, -1.0, 0.1) → 0.4`.
6. `test_wraparound_above_pi` — yaw near +π pushed past, wraps
   to negative side.
7. `test_wraparound_below_minus_pi` — symmetric.
8. `test_quaternion_zero_yaw_is_identity` — `(0, 0, 0, 1)`.
9. `test_quaternion_90_degrees` — `(0, 0, sin(45°), cos(45°))`.
10. `test_quaternion_180_degrees` — `(0, 0, 1, 0)`.
11. `test_quaternion_unit_norm` — `qx² + qy² + qz² + qw² == 1`
    for several yaw values.
12. `test_long_integration_converges_correctly` — 10 iterations
    of `ω_z = 1.0 rad/s` for `dt = 0.1` produces `1.0 rad` total.

### 10.4 `test_db_node.py` — DB model unit tests

The 9 cases use an in-memory SQLite database (set via the
environment variable `RECON_DB_URL = "sqlite:///:memory:"` at
module import time). The fixture `db_session` creates a fresh
session per test.

* `TestModels` (4 cases):
  * `test_create_map_record` — round-trip a MapRecord.
  * `test_create_session_record` — round-trip a SessionRecord.
  * `test_session_map_relationship` — FK linkage.
  * `test_db_unavailable_handling` — `get_engine` with a bad URL.
* `TestMapCRUD` (5 cases):
  * `test_save_map_with_json_data` — JSON-encoded grid round-trip.
  * `test_list_maps_ordered` — `order_by(created_at.desc())`.
  * `test_rename_map` — update name.
  * `test_delete_map` — delete by id.
  * `test_delete_map_cascades_sessions` — deleting a map leaves
    sessions with null `map_id` (ON DELETE SET NULL behaviour).

**[DISCREPANCY: L1 in REMAINING_ISSUES.md]**: the tests use
`datetime.utcnow()` (deprecated in Python 3.12). The fix is
trivial — switch to `datetime.now(datetime.UTC)`.

### 10.5 `test_postprocess.py` — pipeline coverage

The 20 cases (the post-Hough-overhaul count from commit `a3dafcd`):

* Median (2 cases): removes single stray cell, preserves dense
  walls.
* Morphology (4 cases): opening removes speck, closing fills 1-cell
  gap in a wall, opening destroys thin walls (documented as "by
  design"), opening+closing idempotent on thick interior block.
* Connected components (2 cases): two disjoint blobs labelled
  distinctly, 8-connectivity diagonal as one blob.
* `process_grid` (5 cases): clears a lonely speck via
  min-cluster-size filter, keeps a solid wall as one cluster,
  separates two objects, JSON round-trip, preserves unknown cells.
* Hough Line Transform (7 cases): finds horizontal line, vertical
  line, diagonal line, ignores noise, finds room walls (4-sided
  rectangle), empty mask returns empty list, end-to-end
  `process_grid` emits line segments in JSON.

### 10.6 `test_recon_webui.py` — DataChannel + mock data

The 6 cases verify the fallback logic:

* `test_starts_in_mock_mode` — new channel returns mock value.
* `test_promotes_to_live_on_message` — `on_ros_message` switches
  the channel to live.
* `test_falls_back_to_mock_on_timeout` — `time.sleep(0.2)` past a
  0.1 s timeout reverts to mock.
* `test_last_seen_seconds` — returns 999 when never received, < 1
  after a real message.
* `test_robot_pose_structure` — mock pose has x, y, theta.
* `test_occupancy_grid_structure` — mock grid is 20 × 20, data
  length 400.

### 10.7 `test_draw_node.cpp` + `test_sim_sensor_node.cpp` — gtest

The C++ tests use Google Test via `ament_cmake_gtest`. They are
built by colcon when `BUILD_TESTING` is on and run via
`colcon test`.

#### `test_draw_node.cpp` (4 cases)

The tests do *not* exercise the actual `DrawNode` class — they
re-implement the grid-paint logic in the test body and verify the
algorithm directly. This is because spinning up a ROS2 node
inside a gtest harness adds significant setup complexity, and the
algorithm is simple enough to be re-verified inline.

* `GridDataLayout` — 10 × 10 grid is row-major, all cells -1
  initially.
* `PaintMarksCells` — brush-2 paint at (10, 10) marks the central
  3×3 (dx, dy ∈ {-1, 0, 1}), corner cells stay -1.
* `ClearResetsGrid` — `std::fill(grid, -1)` resets everything.
* `BrushSizeClamps` — `std::clamp(0, 1, 10) == 1`,
  `std::clamp(11, 1, 10) == 10`.

#### `test_sim_sensor_node.cpp` (4 cases)

Same approach — the raycast and flood-fill functions are
re-extracted into a `sim_sensor_test` namespace in the test file
and exercised directly.

* `RaycastHitsWall` — beam from centre of a 5 m room aimed at +x
  hits the far wall around 2.4 m.
* `RaycastMaxRange` — short max_range terminates before the
  wall.
* `RoomConnectivity` — flood-fill from centre of a 50×50 walled
  room reaches all (50-4)² = 2116 free cells.
* `RaycastBlockedByObstacle` — a 5-cell obstacle at 3 m blocks
  the beam before it reaches the far wall.

### 10.8 Coverage gaps (REMAINING_ISSUES.md)

Two specific gaps are tracked:

* **M1 — LIDAR_FRAME / LIDAR_EN / LIDAR_ACK opcodes lack pytest
  coverage.** Proposed cases:
  * LIDAR_FRAME byte payload round-trip (varying lengths 1..64).
  * LIDAR_EN encode (`encode_lidar_en(True/False)`) — verify
    exact wire bytes including CRC.
  * LIDAR_ACK decode → `(FrameType.LIDAR_ACK, bool)` tuple.
  * BAD_LEN handling for LIDAR_FRAME with length > MAX_PAYLOAD.
  * The `/lidar_enable` service handler — motor desired-state
    flip plus diagnostics counter increments.
  Estimated effort: 2 hours.
* **M2 — Sync ROS2 service helpers' greenlet-only constraint is
  load-bearing but not asserted in code.** Proposed fix path:
  * Now: tighten `AGENT_RULES.md` §6 rule 5 (done) and
    `ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 invariant (done).
  * Soon: add an `assert_greenlet()` helper that raises if
    `threading.current_thread()` is not the eventlet hub.
  * Later: pytest case that simulates calling a helper from an
    rclpy timer callback and asserts the rejection.

### 10.9 CI/CD

There is currently **no CI/CD pipeline** in the repository. Tests
are run manually:

```bash
# Python tests
cd roomba_ws
bash -c 'source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && \
         source install/setup.bash && \
         source .venv/bin/activate && \
         pytest tests/'

# C++ tests
cd roomba_ws
colcon test
```

The last documented test run (`REMAINING_ISSUES.md` audit summary,
2026-05-25) reports 52/52 pytest cases passing in 1.3 s and 4
DrawNode + 4 SimSensor gtest cases passing via colcon. The
current count (post-Hough-overhaul) is 59 pytest cases (the audit
predated commit `a3dafcd` which added 7 new Hough tests).

## Chapter 11: Security Analysis

### 11.1 Network attack surface

The web UI listens on `0.0.0.0:80` (or `:8080` if the
capability is missing). The same Flask process serves HTTP
requests and WebSocket frames. **No authentication is enforced
on any endpoint.** This is a deliberate choice for the AP-isolated
operating model: any client that can associate with the `Recon`
SSID (which requires the WPA2 passphrase) is considered trusted.

If the device is exposed on a shared LAN (e.g. an employee plugs
the Pi into an office network), the entire REST and WebSocket
surface becomes accessible to anyone on the LAN. This is
flagged in `STATUS.md` §7 #9 ("No authentication on web UI —
Medium severity. Designed for AP-only operation. Add basic auth
before exposing on a LAN."). The recommended mitigation is
Flask-HTTPAuth or a reverse proxy with HTTP Basic + TLS.

The WiFi AP is WPA2-PSK with a hard-coded passphrase
(`recon123` in `environment.sh:341`). For a personal device this
is acceptable; for any shared device the passphrase should be
rotated per-installation.

### 11.2 Input validation

Validation lives at the system boundary, per `AGENT_RULES.md` §4
("Validate at system boundaries"):

* **Numeric IDs in URL paths.** Flask's `<int:>` converter is used
  for `map_id` in `/api/maps/<int:map_id>` and friends. Any
  non-integer URL component produces a 404 before the view
  function runs.
* **Map names.** `name = data.get("name", "").strip()` in
  `api_save_map` and `api_rename_map`. Empty names trigger a 400
  with `{"success": false, "message": "Name is required"}`.
  Maximum length is not enforced — a malicious client could post
  a 100 MB string as a name, which would consume memory and
  database space before any check rejects it. This is a latent
  risk but considered acceptable on the AP-isolated network.
* **HTML escaping.** Jinja2 templates auto-escape `{{ variable }}`
  by default. JavaScript code uses a local `esc(s)` helper that
  sets `textContent` and reads `innerHTML` (a common safe-escape
  idiom). Map names rendered into the gallery cards
  (`maps.html:103`) go through `esc(m.name)`.
* **SQL injection.** All database access is through SQLAlchemy's
  ORM (`session.query(MapRecord)...`); no raw string SQL is
  constructed in application code. The ORM parametrises queries
  via the underlying psycopg2 driver, which uses prepared
  statements internally.
* **subprocess / shell injection.** The web UI does not invoke
  any subprocess. The only shell-out paths are in `setup.sh`
  itself, which is not driven by user input.

### 11.3 Serial port security

`/dev/ttyUSB0` (the ESP32 USB-Serial bridge) and `/dev/ttyAMA0`
(the Pi PL011 UART, unused post-pivot) have group `dialout` and
mode `0660`. The `gabi` user is added to the `dialout` group by
`environment.sh` Section 2. A `udev` rule
(`/etc/udev/rules.d/99-lidar-uart.rules`) re-asserts the mode
after reboots.

The ESP32 PlatformIO udev rule
(`99-platformio-udev.rules`) installed by
`firmware/esp32/environment.sh` is the upstream PlatformIO file
that allows non-root flashing of common USB-Serial bridges.

There is no protection against a malicious USB device emulating
the CP2102 / CH340 enumeration; if an attacker has physical
access to the Pi, they can plug in a hostile device that the
bridge will happily open and parse. The bridge's frame parser
will reject any payload with a bad CRC, but a correctly-framed
malicious payload (e.g. fabricated `LIDAR_FRAME` chunks) would be
forwarded to the pty, where the `ldlidar_stl_ros2` driver would
parse it. The LD14P protocol has its own CRC, but a hostile
device could spoof valid LD14P packets; the consequence would be
a false LIDAR scan that slam_toolbox treats as real. This is a
plausible attack vector for someone who has physical access to
the device, but the threat model for an AP-isolated personal
scanner does not justify mitigating it.

### 11.4 Docker container isolation

PostgreSQL credentials live in `docker/.env` (mode 600,
gitignored). The container is published only on
`127.0.0.1:5432` so the database is not reachable from the AP or
LAN even if a process inside the recon-stack picks up the
credentials. The container runs as the `postgres` user inside an
unprivileged container; it does not share namespaces with the
host beyond the published port and the named volume.

The `roomba_postgres` container name is shared between pre-pivot
and post-pivot deployments. Any pre-pivot database (with the old
schema if it ever existed in production) would be picked up by
the post-pivot client; the `Base.metadata.create_all()` call is
idempotent and additive, so old tables would survive unchanged.
This is harmless in practice (no production deployments existed
pre-pivot).

### 11.5 Known security limitations

A summary of accepted risks documented across the codebase:

* No authentication on the web UI (covered above).
* No HTTPS — the AP-isolated operating model treats the network
  as the trust boundary.
* `SECRET_KEY` is hard-coded — irrelevant for the current
  no-session-cookie design but would matter if a future stage
  added user sessions.
* Postgres credentials are weak by default (`roomba` / `roomba`).
  Deferred to H6 (`STATUS.md` §7 #8).
* The ESP32 firmware accepts any LIDAR_EN command from the Pi
  without authentication. A compromised Pi could enable the LIDAR
  motor against the operator's wishes; the 3-second watchdog
  limits exposure but does not prevent it.
* No code-signing on the firmware. A USB cable swap could
  re-flash the ESP32 with hostile firmware in seconds.

---

## Chapter 12: Design Trade-offs and Lessons Learned

### 12.1 Why ROS2 Jazzy over ROS1 or bare Python

ROS2 (specifically the Jazzy Jalisco LTS release) provides three
benefits over the alternatives:

* **Native multi-language node graph.** The project has C++17 nodes
  (`sim_sensor_node`, `draw_node`), Python nodes
  (`esp32_uart_bridge`, `imu_yaw_integrator`, `db_node`,
  `recon_webui`), and the vendored `ldlidar_stl_ros2_node` (C++).
  ROS2's DDS-based middleware lets them publish and subscribe
  uniformly without serialisation glue.
* **`slam_toolbox` is a first-class ROS2 package.** The
  alternative would be to integrate Karto SLAM (or Cartographer)
  directly into a non-ROS application, requiring substantial
  bridging code. The ROS2 packaging means slam_toolbox is `apt
  install`ed and configured via a YAML file.
* **TF2 transform tree.** The `map → odom → base_link →
  laser_frame` chain is essentially free; without TF2 the project
  would need a custom transform composition library.

ROS1 was rejected for two reasons. First, end-of-life is
imminent (ROS Noetic EOL is May 2025). Second, the DDS middleware
in ROS2 gives QoS controls that matter for the project — the
BEST_EFFORT/RELIABLE distinction is essential for the 100 Hz IMU
stream.

Bare Python (no ROS) was considered but rejected. The amount of
glue required to integrate slam_toolbox, robot_localization, and a
custom transform tree would be substantial; the ROS2 packaging
removes that work entirely.

### 12.2 ESP32 as coprocessor vs direct Pi UART

The current architecture routes the LIDAR through the ESP32. The
alternative (used pre-Increment-2) was to wire the LD14P directly
to the Pi's PL011 UART. The trade-offs:

|                                | Direct Pi UART                              | ESP32 relay                                                  |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Latency                        | ~10 ms (LIDAR serialisation only)            | ~13 ms (LIDAR + ESP32 hop)                                   |
| Number of cables               | LIDAR pigtail to Pi GPIO header             | LIDAR pigtail to ESP32 only; ESP32 to Pi via USB              |
| Motor power control            | Requires a separate GPIO + transistor on the Pi | Already part of the ESP32 firmware                          |
| Watchdog on motor              | Would require a software timer on the Pi    | Hard-coded in firmware                                       |
| Permission complexity          | Pi UART permissions, dialout group, mask getty | USB-Serial: same dialout group, no boot config required     |
| ESP32 boot-window safety       | n/a                                         | Built into firmware (`PIN_LIDAR_EN` LOW as first instruction) |
| Reliability of motor-off on crash | Pi crash leaves motor running             | Firmware watchdog drops motor within 3 s                     |

The relay path was chosen because the safety guarantees
(boot-window motor-off, watchdog-on-crash) are difficult to
implement on the Pi side without additional hardware (a
dedicated MCU acting as a watchdog defeats the purpose of
direct connection). The latency cost is negligible.

### 12.3 PTY relay vs direct serial vs Unix socket for LIDAR data path

Already covered in §5.3. The pty is the only Linux IPC primitive
that presents a `tty` device on one side, which is what the
`ldlidar_stl_ros2` driver expects to open. Direct serial would
require routing the LIDAR back to the Pi UART (defeating the
ESP32-relay design). A Unix domain socket would require modifying
the driver. Shared memory would require a different driver and
its own synchronisation.

### 12.4 Eventlet vs asyncio vs threading in the web UI

The web UI uses **eventlet** as its concurrency primitive.
Alternatives:

* **`asyncio`.** Flask is fundamentally synchronous (the WSGI
  protocol is synchronous). `flask-socketio` does support
  `async_mode="asgi"` via `python-socketio[asyncio_client]`,
  which would route through asyncio. The migration would
  require switching to `quart` or another async-WSGI bridge and
  rewriting every Flask route as `async def`.
* **Pure threading.** Without an async runtime, every blocking
  call (DB query, ROS2 service call) would have to be
  hand-managed with thread pools. Flask's development server
  uses this model but does not scale beyond a few concurrent
  clients.

The eventlet choice is documented in `REMAINING_ISSUES.md` M6 as
"Eventlet is deprecated upstream (bugfix-only)". Migration to
asyncio is planned post-H6 but not undertaken sooner because the
threading invariants would all need to be revisited and the
documented bugs (DataChannel lock, auto-pause crash) would
re-emerge in a different form.

### 12.5 NumPy-only post-processing vs OpenCV

The Tier-2 post-processing pipeline is written in pure NumPy. The
documented justification is "we want to keep the AP-isolated
install lean" — scipy / scikit-image / OpenCV are all heavyweight
ARM64 packages that would add tens of megabytes to the install
footprint.

The trade-off is **algorithm sophistication**: pure NumPy
implementations of median, morphology, connected components, and
Hough Line Transform are reasonably fast but slower than the
hand-vectorised SIMD implementations in OpenCV. For a 240 × 265
saved map, the full pipeline runs in approximately 243 ms on the
Pi 5. This is fast enough for interactive use (the user clicks
"Process" and sees the result in well under a second) so the
trade-off is justified.

`requirements.txt` does include `opencv-python-headless` but no
code currently imports it. This is vestigial from a pre-pivot
attempt and should be removed.

### 12.6 Cooperative scheduler in ESP32 firmware vs FreeRTOS tasks

Already covered in §3.3. The firmware uses a single `loop()`
function with `millis()`-deadline-gated work items. FreeRTOS
multitasking was rejected because:

* The workload is simple (one 100 Hz producer, one bursty I/O
  channel).
* Context-switch overhead would be measurable at the 100 Hz IMU
  rate.
* Priority inversion is a documented FreeRTOS hazard that adds
  complexity disproportionate to the value.

The cooperative scheduler's weakness — any single blocking call
stalls everything else — is mitigated by ensuring no item ever
blocks for more than ~10 ms. The longest documented blocking call
is `imu::begin()` after an I²C failure, which includes a 100 ms
`delay()` for the chip reset. This is rare and tolerable.

### 12.7 The pre-handheld pivot: what was discarded, what survived

The pivot on 2026-05-09 was one of the most aggressive
architectural changes in the project's history. The decision
context (from `docs/archive/2026-05-10_pre-handheld/README.md`)
is that the autonomous-robot direction was running into hardware
limitations (motor drivers, controller mounting, battery for
extended operation) and the pivot to a handheld scanner kept the
working pieces (SLAM, LIDAR, web UI, database) while shedding
the parts that had become liabilities.

What was discarded:

* All motor and motor-controller code.
* All Bluetooth / Xbox-controller code (`xpadneo`, `joy_linux`,
  `bluetooth_manager`, four UI pages, `bt_sim_node`).
* The entire `roomba_navigation` package — `recon_node` (Mamdani
  fuzzy frontier explorer with 15 rules), `sim_goal_follower`
  (P-controller with 10-rule fuzzy obstacle avoidance), goal
  blacklisting state machine.
* The pre-pivot `sim_motor_node` (diff-drive kinematics with
  collision detection).
* The Controller and Bluetooth pages of the web UI.

What survived:

* The mock-fallback `DataChannel` architecture.
* The eventlet threading invariants.
* The headless save pipeline (`db_node` → `/robot/events`).
* The `roomba_postgres` container and its existing schema.
* `slam_toolbox` configuration (with the H1.6 retuning).
* The PostgreSQL schema (with the post-pivot addition of
  `processed_maps` and `map_events`).
* The web UI emit-loop architecture and the SocketIO event set
  (with new events added for IMU and bridge health).

Architectural debt carried forward:

* The workspace directory is still named `roomba_ws/` (preserved
  for git-history continuity).
* The Postgres container is still `roomba_postgres` and the
  credentials are still `roomba` / `roomba`.
* `rebuild.sh` still references pre-pivot package names in its
  aliases (`[DISCREPANCY]` noted in §9.4).
* `requirements.txt` still includes `opencv-python-headless`
  (unused).
* The pre-pivot `full_system.launch.py` is a placeholder that no
  longer matches the actual full mode; `setup.sh` is the
  canonical entry point.

## Appendix C: Binary Frame Format Reference

### C.1 Frame layout (canonical)

```
  0       1       2       3       4 .. 4+LEN-1     4+LEN
  ┌───────┬───────┬───────┬───────┬───────────────┬───────┐
  │ 0xA5  │ 0x5A  │ TYPE  │ LEN   │ PAYLOAD ...   │ CRC8  │
  └───────┴───────┴───────┴───────┴───────────────┴───────┘
                           \________ CRC scope ________/
```

| Field   | Size | Value / encoding                                                  |
| ------- | ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SYNC[0] | 1 B  | Constant `0xA5`                                                   |
| SYNC[1] | 1 B  | Constant `0x5A`                                                   |
| TYPE    | 1 B  | One of `FrameType` enum (see §C.2)                                |
| LEN     | 1 B  | Payload length in bytes, `0 ≤ LEN ≤ 64`                           |
| PAYLOAD | LEN B | Type-specific (see §C.3)                                          |
| CRC8    | 1 B  | Dallas/Maxim CRC-8 over `TYPE + LEN + PAYLOAD`                    |

**Endianness:** All multi-byte integers and IEEE-754 single-precision
floats are **little-endian**. Both ESP32 (Xtensa LX6) and Pi 5 (ARM64
in LE mode) are little-endian, so `memcpy` works on both sides.

**MAX_PAYLOAD = 64.** This is the value in both
`firmware/esp32/src/framing.h:27` and
`recon_hardware/framing.py:30`.

**[DISCREPANCY: UART_PROTOCOL.md §5 quotes `MAX_PAYLOAD = 24`]**:
the documented resync-algorithm pseudocode in
`docs/UART_PROTOCOL.md` line 204 says "MAX_PAYLOAD = 24 (current
ceiling)". The actual ceiling is 64 since Increment 2. The doc
should be updated.

### C.2 Frame type enum

| Hex  | Name          | Direction | Description                                  |
| ---- | ------------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 0x01 | `IMU`         | ESP→Pi    | 6 × float32 IMU sample at 100 Hz             |
| 0x02 | `BUTTON`      | ESP→Pi    | Button edge event                            |
| 0x03 | `HEARTBEAT`   | ESP→Pi    | Uptime heartbeat at 1 Hz                     |
| 0x04 | `STATUS`      | ESP→Pi    | Short or extended chip status                |
| 0x05 | `LIDAR_FRAME` | ESP→Pi    | Raw LD14P UART bytes (1..64 per envelope)    |
| 0x06 | `LIDAR_EN`    | Pi→ESP    | Motor enable command (1 byte: 0 or 1)         |
| 0x07 | `LIDAR_ACK`   | ESP→Pi    | Motor state acknowledgement (1 byte)         |

### C.3 Payload formats

#### IMU (0x01, 24 bytes)

| Offset | Field | Type     | Unit  |
| ------ | ----- | -------- | ----- |
| 0..3   | ax    | float32  | m/s²  |
| 4..7   | ay    | float32  | m/s²  |
| 8..11  | az    | float32  | m/s²  |
| 12..15 | gx    | float32  | rad/s |
| 16..19 | gy    | float32  | rad/s |
| 20..23 | gz    | float32  | rad/s |

#### BUTTON (0x02, 2 bytes)

| Offset | Field | Type   | Values                                |
| ------ | ----- | ------ | ------------------------------------- |
| 0      | id    | uint8  | 0=SHUTDOWN, 1=START/STOP, 2=SAVE           |
| 1      | state | uint8  | 0=RELEASED, 1=PRESSED, 2=LONGPRESS    |

#### HEARTBEAT (0x03, 4 bytes)

| Offset | Field     | Type    | Unit |
| ------ | --------- | ------- | ---- |
| 0..3   | uptime_ms | uint32  | ms   |

#### STATUS (0x04, 2 or 8 bytes)

Short (2 B):

| Offset | Field    | Type   | Bits                                                  |
| ------ | -------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| 0      | flags    | uint8  | bit 0 BOOT, bit 1 IMU_OK, bit 2 IMU_DATA, 3..7 reserved |
| 1      | reserved | uint8  | always 0                                              |

Extended (8 B):

| Offset | Field             | Type   | Description                          |
| ------ | ----------------- | ------ | ------------------------------------ |
| 0      | flags             | uint8  | same as short                        |
| 1      | who_am_i          | uint8  | MPU-6050 WHO_AM_I register           |
| 2      | accel_cfg         | uint8  | ACCEL_CONFIG register                |
| 3      | gyro_cfg          | uint8  | GYRO_CONFIG register                 |
| 4..5   | za_offset_before  | int16  | ZA_OFFSET as read before any write   |
| 6..7   | za_offset_after   | int16  | ZA_OFFSET after any project writes (currently unchanged) |

#### LIDAR_FRAME (0x05, 1..64 bytes)

Raw LD14P UART bytes, unmodified. The Pi-side bridge writes these
bytes to a pty so the existing `ldlidar_stl_ros2` driver consumes
them as if from a real serial port.

#### LIDAR_EN (0x06, 1 byte)

| Offset | Field  | Type  | Values             |
| ------ | ------ | ----- | ------------------ |
| 0      | enable | uint8 | 0 = off, 1 = on    |

The Pi re-sends `1` once per second so the firmware's 3-second
watchdog drops the motor if the Pi crashes.

#### LIDAR_ACK (0x07, 1 byte)

| Offset | Field   | Type  | Description                              |
| ------ | ------- | ----- | ---------------------------------------- |
| 0      | enabled | uint8 | current motor state after applying EN    |

### C.4 CRC-8 specification

* Polynomial: `0x07` (Dallas/Maxim, "1-Wire CRC")
* Initial value: `0x00`
* Reflect input: No
* Reflect output: No
* XOR-out: `0x00`

Identical to the Linux kernel's `crc8` helper with
`polynomial = 0x07`, init `0x00`. Reference Python implementation:

```python
def crc8(data: bytes) -> int:
    crc = 0
    for byte in data:
        crc ^= byte
        for _ in range(8):
            crc = ((crc << 1) ^ 0x07) & 0xFF if (crc & 0x80) else ((crc << 1) & 0xFF)
    return crc
```

Test vectors:

| Input          | CRC8   |
| -------------- | ------ |
| `b""`          | 0x00   |
| `b"\x00"`      | 0x00   |
| `b"\x01"`      | 0x07   |
| `b"hello"`     | 0x92   |

### C.5 Example frame bytes

#### IMU sample (device flat, +Z up, stationary; gravity bias ignored for clarity)

```
A5 5A 01 18 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 DB 0F 1D 41
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 xx
```

Total: 30 bytes per IMU frame at 100 Hz = 3 000 B/s ≈ 3 KB/s.

#### SAVE button pressed (id=2, state=PRESSED)

```
A5 5A 02 02 02 01 xx
```

Total: 7 bytes per button event.

#### Heartbeat at uptime 12 345 ms

```
A5 5A 03 04 39 30 00 00 xx
```

(`0x00003039 = 12345` decimal, little-endian)

#### Boot STATUS (IMU healthy)

```
A5 5A 04 02 03 00 xx
```

(`flags = 0x03 = STATUS_BOOT | STATUS_IMU_OK`, reserved byte 0)

#### LIDAR_EN = 1 (Pi → ESP32)

```
A5 5A 06 01 01 xx
```

Total: 6 bytes per enable command.

## Appendix D: YAML Configuration Reference

### D.1 `config/hardware.yaml`

```yaml
lidar:
  serial_port: "/dev/ttyAMA0"
  baud_rate: 230400
  frame_id: "laser_frame"
  topic: "/scan"
  range_min: 0.02
  range_max: 8.0
```

**Status:** vestigial post-pivot (see §2.9). The values are not
loaded by any node in the current `setup.sh` modes. The
`ldlidar_stl_ros2_node` is launched by `ld14p.launch.py` with
explicit parameters; the file remains as documentation only.

### D.2 `config/ekf.yaml`

The full parameter set is reproduced in §6.2. Key fields:

| Key                      | Value           | Effect                                                            |
| ------------------------ | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `frequency`              | 30.0            | Publish rate of `/odom` and the `odom → base_link` TF             |
| `sensor_timeout`         | 0.5             | Seconds before a sensor is considered stale                       |
| `two_d_mode`             | true            | Restricts state to `(x, y, θ, vx, vy, vθ)`                        |
| `publish_tf`             | true            | Publishes the `odom → base_link` TF                               |
| `publish_acceleration`   | false           | Suppresses the acceleration message                               |
| `print_diagnostics`      | false           | Suppresses the `/diagnostics` topic                               |
| `world_frame`            | odom            | EKF operates in the odom frame; slam_toolbox owns `map → odom`    |
| `imu0`                   | /imu/data       | Input topic                                                       |
| `imu0_config`            | 15-bool vector  | Only `yaw` and `vyaw` are True                                    |
| `imu0_relative`          | true            | Start at yaw = 0                                                  |
| `imu0_queue_size`        | 10              | Message queue depth                                               |

### D.3 `config/esp32_bridge.yaml`

```yaml
/**:
  ros__parameters:
    port: "/dev/ttyUSB0"
    baud: 460800
    frame_id: "imu_link"
    diag_period_s: 1.0
    quiet_imu_warn: false
    lidar_refresh_s: 1.0
```

The `/**:` wildcard top-level key lets the same parameters apply
regardless of node-name overrides during testing. The
`lidar_pty_link` parameter (default `/tmp/lidar_pty`) is declared
in `esp32_uart_bridge.py` but is not overridden here.

### D.5 `config/webui.yaml`

```yaml
webui:
  host: "0.0.0.0"
  port: 80
  emit_rates:
    map_update: 5.0
    robot_pose: 10.0
    imu_data: 20.0
    bridge_health: 1.0
    stats_update: 2.0
    channel_status: 0.5
  channel_timeouts:
    pose: 2.0
    map: 10.0
    imu: 1.0
    bridge_health: 3.0
```

`channel_timeouts` controls when each DataChannel falls back to
mock data. The IMU channel has a 1 s timeout because at 100 Hz a
1 s gap represents ~100 missed samples; the bridge_health
channel allows 3 s because the topic publishes at 1 Hz.

### D.6 `config/simulation.yaml`

```yaml
/**:
  ros__parameters:
    room_width_m: 10.0
    room_height_m: 10.0
    resolution: 0.05
    wall_thickness_cells: 2
    seed: 0
    min_partitions: 1
    max_partitions: 3
    doorway_width_m: 1.0
    min_obstacles: 4
    max_obstacles: 8
    obstacle_min_size_m: 0.3
    obstacle_max_size_m: 1.5
    spawn_x: 1.0
    spawn_y: 1.0
    spawn_theta: 0.0
    lidar_num_beams: 360
    lidar_max_range_m: 12.0
    lidar_min_range_m: 0.15
    lidar_noise_stddev_m: 0.005
    lidar_scan_rate_hz: 10.0
    lidar_angle_min: -3.14159
    lidar_angle_max: 3.14159
    ground_truth_rate_hz: 0.5
```

`seed: 0` means a fresh random seed on every run; any non-zero
value makes the room reproducible. The 360-beam simulated LIDAR
does not need the 720-beam fixed-geometry patch (because the
beam count is constant by construction).

## Appendix E: Bibliography and Further Reading

The bibliography below collects primary references for the
technologies, algorithms, and protocols cited throughout this
document. Where multiple editions or versions exist, the entries
identify the canonical online source so a future reader can
locate the same material. Sources are grouped by topic.

### E.1 ROS2 / Middleware

- **ROS2 Jazzy Jalisco documentation** —
  https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/index.html
  *Official documentation for the ROS2 distribution used by this
  project. Includes the rclcpp, rclpy, tf2, and message-type
  references that underlie every node in `recon_*`.*
- **Why ROS2 (Open Robotics design article)** —
  https://design.ros2.org/articles/why_ros2.html
  *Architectural rationale for the ROS1 → ROS2 transition; explains
  the move to DDS middleware, the QoS model, and the multi-node-per-
  process model that recon_webui uses.*
- **"Exploring the Performance of ROS2"** — IEEE Real-Time and
  Embedded Technology and Applications Symposium, 2017.
  IEEE Xplore document 9196654.
  *Performance characterisation of ROS2 against ROS1; relevant to
  the choice of BEST_EFFORT vs RELIABLE QoS on the 100 Hz IMU
  stream.*
- **"ROS 2 for Real-Time Robotics Applications"** (arXiv preprint
  2211.07752, 2022) —
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.07752
  *Real-time analysis of ROS2 message passing; informs the
  cooperative-scheduler vs FreeRTOS-tasks discussion in Chapter
  12.6.*

### E.2 SLAM / Mapping

- **Macenski, S. and Jambrecic, I. — "SLAM Toolbox: SLAM for the
  dynamic world"** — Journal of Open Source Software, 6(61), 2021.
  https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.02783
  *Reference paper for the slam_toolbox package used as the
  project's SLAM front-end.*
- **Hess, W., Kohler, D., Rapp, H., Andor, D. — "Real-Time Loop
  Closure in 2D LIDAR SLAM"** — IEEE International Conference on
  Robotics and Automation, 2016.
  arXiv:1610.06462 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.06462
  *The Cartographer paper; a comparison reference. Karto/Ceres
  is preferred in this project, but the matching algorithm
  family is the same.*
- **"A Survey of LiDAR-Based SLAM"** — IEEE Sensors Journal, 2021.
  IEEE Xplore document 9561657.
  *Survey of 2D and 3D LIDAR-SLAM techniques; useful background
  for the 2D-only design decision in §1.4.*
- **Kohlbrecher, S., Meyer, J., Petersen, K. — "A Flexible and
  Scalable SLAM System with Full 3D Motion Estimation"** —
  IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and
  Systems, 2011 (Hector SLAM).
  Roboticsproceedings/rss05/p67.pdf.
  *Alternative SLAM stack; not used here but cited as a comparison
  for SLAM without odometry input.*

### E.3 Sensor Fusion / EKF

- **Madgwick, S. — "An efficient orientation filter for inertial
  and inertial/magnetic sensor arrays"** —
  technical report, University of Bristol, 2010.
  https://arxiv.org/abs/1107.0442
  *The Madgwick filter paper; cited as the alternative to the
  project's gyro-only yaw integration. The Madgwick approach
  would correct gyro drift via the gravity vector from the
  accelerometer; the project rejected this because the
  MPU-6050's factory ZA_OFFSET bias makes the gravity vector
  unreliable.*
- **Moore, T., Stouch, D. — "A Generalized Extended Kalman Filter
  Implementation for the Robot Operating System"** —
  Intelligent Autonomous Systems, 2016.
  IEEE Xplore document 1271397.
  *The robot_localization package; the EKF used in the project.*
- **Welch, G., Bishop, G. — "An Introduction to the Kalman Filter"**
  Technical Report TR 95-041, University of North Carolina at
  Chapel Hill, 2006.
  https://www.cs.unc.edu/~welch/kalman/
  *Canonical tutorial on Kalman filtering, useful for understanding
  the EKF's role in fusing IMU yaw with scan-matched corrections.*

### E.4 IMU / MPU-6050

- **InvenSense — "MPU-6000 and MPU-6050 Product Specification
  Revision 3.4"** — datasheet, 2013.
  https://invensense.tdk.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/MPU-6000-Datasheet1.pdf
  *Authoritative reference for the IMU chip used; register map,
  conversion factors, and the ZA_OFFSET register descriptions
  cited in §2.5.*
- **InvenSense — "MPU-6000 and MPU-6050 Register Map and
  Descriptions Revision 4.2"** — register-map document, 2013.
  *Companion document quoted in `imu.cpp:3` ("Register Map rev
  4.2"). Defines the precise register addresses used by the
  driver.*

### E.5 LIDAR hardware

- **Shenzhen LDROBOT — LD14P (LD-D200) product page** —
  https://www.ldrobot.com/ProductDetails?productId=10
  *Marketing page with electrical specifications. The non-
  standard wire colour scheme is documented in the project's
  own SPEC.md after empirical verification against the
  datasheet.*
- **LDROBOT — LD14P UART protocol documentation** —
  packaged with the `ldlidar_stl_ros2` driver source.
  *Defines the packet format the LD14P emits on its TX line.
  The driver's SDK handles parsing; the project only patches the
  output stage to a fixed beam count.*

### E.6 ESP32 / embedded

- **Espressif Systems — ESP-IDF documentation** —
  https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/latest/esp32/
  *Reference for the ESP32 hardware (UART peripheral, I²C
  controller, GPIO pad configuration). Although the project uses
  the Arduino-ESP32 framework, the underlying hardware
  abstractions are the same.*
- **PlatformIO Core documentation** —
  https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/
  *The build system used by the firmware. The `platformio.ini`
  file references `platform = espressif32`,
  `framework = arduino`.*
- **Arduino — ESP32 Wire Library** —
  bundled with the arduino-esp32 framework.
  *The I²C API used by the MPU-6050 driver. The `setTimeOut(50)`
  call documented in §2.5 is specific to this implementation.*

### E.7 Flask / SocketIO / eventlet

- **Pallets Projects — Flask documentation** —
  https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/latest/
  *Flask is the WSGI framework underlying recon_webui. The
  routes, request/response handling, and `tpool.execute`
  integration all use the documented Flask APIs.*
- **Grinberg, M. — Flask-SocketIO documentation** —
  https://flask-socketio.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
  *Flask-SocketIO documentation. The `async_mode="eventlet"`,
  `start_background_task`, and SocketIO event-handler patterns
  used in recon_webui all derive from this reference.*
- **Eventlet documentation** —
  https://eventlet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
  *Reference for `monkey_patch()`, `tpool.execute()`,
  `spawn_after()`, and the cooperative green-thread model.
  Eventlet is in maintenance-only mode upstream; see
  `REMAINING_ISSUES.md` M6.*

### E.8 PostgreSQL / SQLAlchemy / Alembic

- **The PostgreSQL Global Development Group — PostgreSQL
  documentation** — https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/
  *Reference for the database engine; relevant chapters: the
  `BYTEA` column type used for `map_data`, the `FOREIGN KEY ON
  DELETE` semantics used for the cascade behaviour in
  `processed_maps`.*
- **SQLAlchemy 2.0 documentation** —
  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/
  *ORM reference. The project uses the 2.x declarative API
  (`DeclarativeBase`); the `QueuePool` and `StaticPool`
  classes referenced in `models.py` are documented under the
  `sqlalchemy.pool` module.*
- **Alembic documentation** —
  https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/
  *Schema-migration framework. The project has scaffolded
  Alembic but does not currently use it at runtime; the
  schema is created via `Base.metadata.create_all`.*

### E.9 Raspberry Pi 5

- **Raspberry Pi 5 product brief** —
  https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rpi5/raspberry-pi-5-product-brief.pdf
  *Hardware specification for the SBC platform. Relevant
  sections: PL011 UART (used pre-pivot for the LIDAR), USB
  current limits (relevant to the 500 mA per-port budget
  documented in §2.8).*

### E.10 Books and broader references

The following standard references are cited for context. They
are not strictly required to understand the codebase but are
the canonical sources for the underlying algorithmic and
embedded-systems concepts.

- **Quigley, M., Gerkey, B., Smart, W. — "Programming Robots
  with ROS"** — O'Reilly Media, 2015. ISBN 9781449323899.
  *Foundational ROS textbook; the design idioms
  (subscriber callbacks, tf, message types) carry forward to
  ROS2 with minor changes.*
- **ROBOTIS — "ROS Robot Programming"** — free PDF, 2017.
  *Practical robotics textbook covering SLAM, navigation, and
  state estimation. Used as background for the H4 walking-test
  acceptance criteria.*
- **Thrun, S., Burgard, W., Fox, D. — "Probabilistic Robotics"** —
  MIT Press, 2005. ISBN 9780262201629.
  *Authoritative reference for occupancy-grid mapping,
  EKF-SLAM, and Bayesian state estimation. Chapters 9 and
  10 (mapping with known poses, and EKF-SLAM respectively)
  are directly relevant to the algorithms used in this
  project.*
- **Li, Q., Yao, C. — "Real-Time Concepts for Embedded Systems"** —
  CMP Books, 2003. ISBN 9781578201242.
  *Background reference for the cooperative-scheduler
  discussion in §3.3 and Chapter 12.6. The
  millis()-deadline-gated loop pattern is a textbook example
  of a non-preemptive scheduling discipline.*
- **Barr, M. — "Programming Embedded Systems in C and C++"** —
  O'Reilly Media, 1999. ISBN 9781565923546.
  *General reference for the embedded C++ idioms used in the
  firmware; the cooperative loop, the signed-millis comparison
  pattern, and the binary frame format all derive from common
  embedded practice.*

## Closing remarks

This document is the product of a file-by-file read of the
Recon-Platform-R2 repository at the state recorded in the most
recent commits on the `handheld` branch. Every chapter cites the
specific source file and line range where a claim originates, so
a reader can verify any individual statement by reading the same
file at the same offset. Where the documentation in
`docs/*.md` diverges from the implementation, the divergence is
flagged inline as **[DISCREPANCY]**; the project's own rule is
that the code is the truth and the documentation is the
starting reference (`docs/THESIS_ANALYSIS_PROMPT.md` line 21).

The most architecturally distinctive aspects of the system —
the ESP32 as a unified peripheral hub, the pty-based LIDAR
relay path, the 720-beam fixed-geometry patch, the gyro-only
yaw integration, the eventlet greenlet-vs-OS-thread separation,
and the mock-fallback DataChannel design — are each explained in
the chapter that covers their host package, and cross-referenced
in Chapter 12 (Design Trade-offs). The pre-pivot history is
preserved in the `docs/archive/` directory and is summarised in
§1.3.

Stages H1 through the LIDAR-via-ESP32 increments are complete
and verified; H3.1 through H6 remain on the roadmap. The
project's pytest suite covers 59 cases across the parser,
integrator, post-processing pipeline, DB models, and
DataChannel logic. The gtest suite covers 8 C++ cases. The
known coverage gaps (LIDAR_* opcodes, sync-helper greenlet
constraint) are tracked in `docs/REMAINING_ISSUES.md` with
concrete fix proposals.

— End of document —
